directions.hypothesis: Within a genus, populations from more contaminated wells carry more defense-gene content than populations from cleaner wells. Pooling by genus hides this, which would explain the absent association in the preplanned genus-level test.
directions.outcomes: Supported if defense content within the same genus rises with local contamination across several genera. Refuted if within-genus populations show no trend, leaving only the covariate-adjusted relaxed-mapping result, which depended on coverage and covariate choice.
directions.prior_work: PMID 35107332 found expanded defense gene sets in contaminated-site Rhodanobacter, and PMID 26583008 compared two wells. This direction tests the gradient across many wells, within genera.
directions.question: At the contaminated Oak Ridge site, is the defense signal carried by shifts within genera, which genus-level summaries would miss?
directions.readiness_basis: Community data in the lakehouse stop at genus level with no strain labels, so within-genus comparison needs new metagenomes; the pangenome step is only a pilot.
directions.test: Step 1, lakehouse: in the Pangenome Collection, compare defense-category gene content of Rhodanobacter genomes from contaminated aquifers with other genomes of the genus, using any isolation-source labels available. The earlier work reported expanded defense gene sets in contaminated-site Rhodanobacter. Step 2, experiment: ENIGMA CORAL names taxa only to genus, so collect shotgun metagenomes from wells spanning the contamination gradient, assemble and bin them, and compare defense genes within the same genus across wells. Include genera the current bridge did not map to the pangenome.
directions.title: Does contamination select defense genes within genera rather than between genera?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether pollutant stress favors phage and mobile-element defense, and whether genus-level community functional proxies are the wrong scale for such questions.

directions.hypothesis: The human-associated enrichment sits in complete, contiguous prophage regions, so it reflects ongoing phage exposure and counter-defense. Domesticated remnants would instead show scattered modules in all habitats.
directions.outcomes: Supported if the habitat gap persists in intact prophages after matching. Refuted if it vanishes once only complete regions are counted, or if genome size alone explains it.
directions.prior_work: PMID 25092302 showed pervasive domestication of defective prophages, and PMID 40639337 described phage counter-defense repertoires. Neither compares intact versus remnant modules between habitats.
directions.question: Does the excess of tail, head and anti-defense modules in human-associated species reflect intact, inducible prophages or scattered domesticated remnants?
directions.readiness_basis: Genomes are available, but dedicated prophage calling has not been run on them.
directions.test: Run a dedicated prophage detector (geNomad or VIBRANT) on genomes from human-associated and freshwater species, matched within genus and within genome-size class. Ask whether tail, head and anti-defense genes sit in complete prophages or as isolated genes. Compare per-genome counts of intact regions and the share of anti-defense genes inside them.
directions.title: Are human-associated prophage tail and anti-defense modules active phages or decaying remnants?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate an arms-race explanation from a bookkeeping artifact, and indicate whether annotation-based prophage counts can be used to infer phage pressure.

directions.hypothesis: Among SNIPE-family proteins, carrier species keep a ManYZ-type transporter more often than expected from relatedness, and in E. coli, SNIPE protection against phages is lost when manYZ is deleted.
directions.outcomes: Supported if co-occurrence beats the relatedness-matched expectation in the SNIPE-family subset and manYZ deletion changes protection in E. coli. Refuted if co-occurrence is random and deletions have no effect. A signal in the full set but not the subset would point to annotation noise.
directions.prior_work: PMID 41741653 showed the membrane nuclease cleaves phage DNA during injection. This direction asks whether the transporter dependence holds across species and after deleting the transporter in E. coli.
directions.question: Across SNIPE-domain proteins, does carriage track the presence of ManYZ-type transporters, and does SNIPE protection in E. coli depend on ManYZ?
directions.readiness_basis: Co-occurrence and the strain scan can be computed now, but the deletion or expression strains need to be built; the lakehouse phage panel covers E. coli only and its SNIPE carriers are unconfirmed.
directions.test: Step 1, lakehouse: in the Pangenome Collection, test co-occurrence of SNIPE-domain clusters (4,572 clusters across 1,696 species; an estimated 3,675, or 80.4%, are SNIPE-family proteins, while the other ~897 may be non-SNIPE multi-domain proteins or annotation noise) with ManYZ-type transporter clusters, against relatedness-matched species. Run the full set and the estimated SNIPE-family subset separately. Check Fitness Browser data for E. coli K-12, where manX, manY and manZ show severe defects in few conditions. Scan the 188 E. coli strains in the PhageFoundry Browsers susceptibility collection for the SNIPE domain; carriers are not yet established. Step 2, experiment: in a carrier, delete manYZ and SNIPE singly and together; if none exist, express SNIPE from a plasmid with and without manYZ. Score the panel phages. Klebsiella is not tested, since panel and fitness data there do not exist.
directions.title: Does the SNIPE anti-phage nuclease depend on the mannose transporter ManYZ in E. coli?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that membrane defense nucleases are tied to their phages' entry route, and would predict which hosts SNIPE can protect.

directions.hypothesis: Lipid-A-free Caulobacter survives only if cbb3-type respiration stays on. The sspB deletion helps maintain it when Fur is lost, so supplying the operon should partly replace the need for the sspB deletion.
directions.outcomes: Supported if viability tracks respiratory operon expression and operon supply substitutes for the sspB deletion. Refuted if rescue works with the operon silenced, or if operon supply gives no benefit.
directions.prior_work: PMID 35649364 linked fur loss and anionic sphingolipids to lipid A dispensability and PMIDs 19520766 and 30210482 defined the Fur regulon. None tests respiratory chain requirement.
directions.question: Does the Fur-repressed micro-aerobic respiratory operon, which the sspB deletion buffers at the transcript level, actually matter for survival of lipid-A-free cells?
directions.readiness_basis: Needs new strain constructions; existing transcript data show buffering but do not establish that these genes are required for rescue.
directions.test: In the Caulobacter ΔlpxC background, test viability with fur deleted alone, sspB deleted alone, and both. In ΔfurΔlpxC, express the cbb3/cyd/fix operon (CCNA_01466-01476) from an inducible promoter and score rescue without the sspB deletion. Measure oxygen consumption in each strain, and sphingolipid pools, noting that earlier transcripts came only from rich PYE medium.
directions.title: Is the Fur-controlled respiratory operon needed for lipid A loss in Caulobacter?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether lipid A dispensability is a coupled envelope and energy-state change, rather than only a sphingolipid effect. The buffered transcripts so far only show buffering, not a requirement, and no induction of sphingolipid genes was seen in rich medium.

directions.hypothesis: Suppression needs live commensal cells consuming PA14's preferred substrates. Cell-free spent medium will not suppress, and adding back the depleted substrates will restore PA14 growth.
directions.outcomes: Supported if inhibition needs cells and is reversed by substrate add-back. Refuted if spent medium inhibits or add-back changes nothing, pointing to secreted inhibitors.
directions.prior_work: PMID 17873029 described P. aeruginosa carbon preferences in sputum, and PMIDs 27881418 and 35174108 showed commensal inhibition. None tests depletion as the mechanism.
directions.question: Is commensal suppression of P. aeruginosa PA14 driven by community-level depletion of its preferred substrates, given that no single substrate favored commensals?
directions.readiness_basis: Needs new culture experiments; lakehouse data only predict substrate overlap.
directions.test: Co-culture PA14 with Micrococcus luteus, Neisseria mucosa and Streptococcus salivarius, singly and combined, in a sputum-like medium. Compare with cell-free spent medium, and with co-culture supplemented with PA14's preferred substrates. Measure PA14 growth and the pair-wise combined effects that the additive assumption leaves untested.
directions.title: Do cystic fibrosis commensals suppress Pseudomonas by depleting shared nutrients?
directions.why_it_matters: It would define a design rule for probiotic formulations, which would be built around combined substrate coverage rather than a selective prebiotic.

directions.hypothesis: The tryptophan model leans on biosynthesis and uptake genes, so it predicts growth in tryptophan-limited media, not catabolism. Models fitted only on carbon-source labels would lose this accuracy.
directions.outcomes: Supported if biosynthesis genes dominate and the carbon-only model fails. Refuted if degradation genes dominate and predictions still disagree with the 0 of 50 strains.
directions.question: Why is growth on tryptophan well predicted from gene content when 50 P. fluorescens strains did not use it as a carbon source?
directions.readiness_basis: The trained models and growth labels exist but feature attribution must be rerun by condition label.
directions.test: List the gene families that drive the tryptophan model and classify them as biosynthesis, transport or degradation. Retrain using only carbon-source tryptophan labels and compare with the nitrogen-source and rich-medium labels. Score the 50 P. fluorescens strains with each model. Split the Fitness Browser tryptophan genes by whether tryptophan was the carbon or nitrogen source.
directions.title: Is tryptophan growth prediction capturing biosynthesis rather than use as a carbon source?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that high prediction accuracy can reflect the wrong biology and tell users which conditions gene-content models can be trusted for.

directions.hypothesis: Within species whose whole-genome gene content shows no environment link, accessory genes in defense and mobile-element categories still track isolation environment after phylogeny is removed, while housekeeping categories do not.
directions.outcomes: Support: some categories, most likely defense and mobile elements, stand out against the shuffled null in species with no whole-genome environment effect. Refutation: no category beats the null, so the weak environment signal is genuinely weak or limited by the metadata.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 29975997 and 33602135 report weak habitat signal within single species; this tests, across many species at once, whether the signal sits in particular functional categories that a whole-genome measure averages away.
directions.question: Whole-genome gene content barely tracks environment in most species. Does environment instead select particular functional gene categories, such as defense or mobile elements, within species?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene-cluster presence/absence and isolation-source labels already exist for the species analysed in the ecotype work.
directions.test: Take the species in the Pangenome Collection with enough genomes and direct isolation-source labels. Per species, test each accessory gene family and each functional category for association with environment, holding phylogenetic distance fixed. Compare the observed category-level association with a null built by shuffling environment labels among close relatives. Run this for the species, most of those analysed, in which the whole-genome environment effect was absent.
directions.title: Is environmental adaptation hidden in a few gene categories rather than whole genomes?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that the widespread 'environment does not matter' result comes from averaging over all genes. Ecotype studies would then need to be built around specific functions, not whole-genome similarity.

directions.hypothesis: In host-associated species, gene content varies with body site or tissue of isolation more strongly than with geographic or satellite-embedding distance, while in free-living species the reverse holds.
directions.outcomes: Support: body site explains more than embedding distance in host-associated species and not in free-living species. Refutation: body site adds nothing beyond embeddings, or the lifestyle contrast stays absent.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 31227022, 34523223, 32503908 and 36445161 used direct environmental measurements in host systems; this tests whether host microenvironment, not collection coordinates, explains the missing lifestyle contrast in genome-scale data.
directions.question: Why do host-associated and free-living bacteria look equally weak in environment-gene-content links, when published work finds host-associated communities less responsive to the environment? Is collection-site location the wrong variable for hosts?
directions.readiness_basis: Source text exists but body-site harmonisation and per-species distance models must be built.
directions.test: Select species in the Pangenome Collection that have many genomes from both host and non-host sources, including the clinical-heavy species. Harmonise body site or tissue from isolation source and NMDC BioSamples text. For each species, compare how much gene-content distance is explained by body-site labels versus embedding distance, after removing phylogenetic distance. Compare hosts with free-living species.
directions.title: Do host-associated bacteria track host body site rather than geography?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain the null difference between lifestyles as a measurement error and show what environment variable matters for host-associated bacteria.

directions.hypothesis: Warming increases methane oxidation by raising pmoA activity per cell in existing methanotroph populations, with little change in their abundance.
directions.outcomes: Support: higher methane uptake and pmoA transcript-to-DNA ratios in heated soil with similar pmoA DNA. Refutation: uptake follows pmoA DNA abundance, or heated soils show no uptake difference.
directions.prior_work: PMID 38561130 saw higher methane uptake with warming but no rise in pmoA copies in DNA, and PMID 34512564 profiled warming RNA without these genes; this tests the activity-versus-abundance explanation directly.
directions.question: In long-term heated forest soil, methane-oxidation and glyoxylate-cycle transcripts rose under warming in suggestive signals, Actinobacteria rose and Acidobacteria fell, yet the RNA pool was no more warming-sensitive than DNA. Is warming activating a subset of existing organisms?
directions.readiness_basis: Existing data come from one timepoint and the methane-oxidation signals were only suggestive once the many genes tested were taken into account, so new sampling is required.
directions.test: Measure methane uptake and pmoA DNA and RNA from heated and control Harvard Forest soils, both organic and mineral horizons, at several seasons. Include labelled-methane incubations to identify active methanotrophs. Relate transcript-to-DNA ratios to uptake rates. Check in NMDC Multi-omics warming datasets whether pmoA carriers are recovered as genomes.
directions.title: Does warming raise methane oxidation by activating existing methanotrophs rather than growing them?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that warming responses can occur without community turnover, which affects how soil methane sinks are forecast.

directions.hypothesis: ExoS-positive CF isolates form CF-specific clades with more accessory-gene divergence from environmental strains, while ExoU-positive CF isolates sit inside environmental clades.
directions.outcomes: Support: ExoU-positive CF isolates are nested in environmental clades and ExoS-positive isolates form CF-dominated clades. Refutation: both groups are equally mixed with environmental relatives.
directions.prior_work: PMID 19936230 found nearly all CF strains ExoS-positive in a 328-isolate panel, and PMID 42151817 describes co-colonising ExoU and ExoS strains; this asks about origin and adaptation history across thousands of genomes.
directions.question: Most cystic fibrosis Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates carry the ExoS toxin gene, whereas environmental isolates are far more often ExoU-positive. Are the ExoU-positive CF isolates recent environmental immigrants and the ExoS-positive ones long-adapted lung lineages?
directions.readiness_basis: Effector typing and isolation labels exist for thousands of genomes, but a tree-based comparison has not been done.
directions.test: Using the Pangenome Collection and PROTECT Pathogen Browser, build a core-genome tree for the Pseudomonas aeruginosa genomes with environmental metadata. Classify each by effector type and isolation source. Test whether ExoU-positive CF isolates have nearest relatives from environmental sources more often than ExoS-positive CF isolates, and compare accessory gene divergence from the nearest environmental relative.
directions.title: Are ExoU-carrying cystic fibrosis Pseudomonas recent arrivals from the environment?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that toxin type marks adaptation history and that results from the ExoU-positive PA14 strain may not apply to typical CF infections.

directions.hypothesis: After matching for gene length, core genes with very shallow relative depth are at least as often essential or strongly condition-dependent as annotated, deeply represented core genes. Conservation in these proteins then reflects function, not neglect.
directions.outcomes: Support: shallow core genes show strong or essential phenotypes at rates comparable to deep core genes in length-matched comparisons, in balanced genera as well. Refutation: their rates are clearly lower even when length is matched, which would suggest conservation without much measurable importance under lab conditions. If the pattern holds only in the over-represented genera, it reflects sampling and not biology.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29769716 links mutant phenotypes to poorly annotated genes but does not sort genes by sequence-space depth. PMID 34791371 and PMID 41273079 provide structure coverage, not growth importance.
directions.question: Core gene clusters whose sequences have very few relatives in reference sequence space are mostly unannotated. Are they needed for growth as often as deeply represented core genes, or are they largely neutral and merely conserved within a species?
directions.readiness_basis: The shallow-depth core list and the Fitness Browser links already exist, but the join, length matching and phenotype comparison have not been run, and only organisms with fitness data can be tested.
directions.test: Link core gene clusters in the Pangenome Collection to Fitness Browser genes. Split them into shallow-depth and deep-depth classes and compare the share with strong fitness effects in at least one condition and the share that are essential. Match on gene length, because short genes are poorly measured, and stratify by annotation tier and by organism. Depth was looked up only for each cluster's representative sequence, so check a sample of clusters for member-level diversity. Run the comparison on genera with balanced genome sampling, to see whether the over-represented genera drive the pattern.
directions.title: Do conserved proteins with almost no relatives elsewhere matter for growth?
directions.why_it_matters: The census counts 415,603 shallow core clusters, 68.9% of them hypothetical, and reads conservation as importance without measuring it. That census also rests on a genome collection in which Pseudomonas and E. coli are over-represented, so part of the pattern may reflect sampling. If shallow core genes are often needed for growth, they become high-value targets for structure and function work. If not, conservation alone is a poor guide for choosing targets.

directions.hypothesis: Truly dark genes are mostly recent additions. They differ from their host genome in GC and codon use and are patchily present among close relatives, even when compared with length-matched annotation-lag genes.
directions.outcomes: Support: truly dark genes deviate from the host genome in composition and are patchily present, within Pseudomonadota as well as overall. Refutation: they match the host genome and are present across relatives, which points to fast-evolving old genes. The 17,479 unlinked dark genes cannot be assessed, so the result applies only to the linked set.
directions.prior_work: PMID 38977308 compares species-specific orphan genes with conserved genes in gut genomes. This direction instead compares persistently dark genes with genes that were later annotated, in organisms with fitness data.
directions.question: Genes that stay unannotated after modern reannotation are shorter, more accessory, and have narrower ortholog breadth than genes that were later annotated. Does that pattern mark recent origin (transfer or de novo birth), or old genes that evolve too fast to be recognised?
directions.readiness_basis: Truly dark gene lists and pangenome links exist, but composition and distribution metrics must be computed, and the 17,479 unlinked dark genes cannot be assessed.
directions.test: In the Pangenome Collection, compare truly dark genes with length-matched annotation-lag genes. Measure GC and codon-use deviation from the host genome, patchiness of presence among genomes of the same genus, and neighbouring mobile-element annotations. Treat the Methanococcus strains, which hold 55% of truly dark genes, as a separate stratum, and run the comparison again within Pseudomonadota only. Then check whether profile or structure searches find remote relatives for the host-typical, narrowly distributed subset.
directions.title: Are persistently unannotated genes young lineage-specific inventions or fast-evolving old genes?
directions.why_it_matters: More than half of the ortholog groups of dark genes were classed as kingdom-level, but that rests on 48 Fitness Browser organisms, mostly Pseudomonadota, with several major phyla absent. It also covers a different gene population from the truly dark set. Showing which kind of gene dominates the truly dark set tells experimenters whether to chase niche-specific gains or divergent core functions, and tells annotators whether structure-based search can recover them.

directions.hypothesis: Within organisms that have deep condition panels, truly dark genes with strong phenotypes are co-fitness partners of uptake and transport genes more often than annotation-lag genes are, and show phenotypes more often in nutrient and iron screens than in matched stress screens.
directions.outcomes: Support: after alignment, truly dark genes still show less stress and more nutrient and iron phenotypes than annotation-lag genes, co-vary with uptake genes, and show phenotypes more often in nutrient and iron screens. Refutation: the contrast shrinks or reverses with common definitions or within deep-panel organisms, partners are mostly stress genes, or nutrient and iron screens find no more phenotypes than stress screens.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29769716 and PMID 22125499 tie poorly annotated genes to conditions but do not compare condition classes between truly dark and annotation-lag genes. This direction adds a proposed function class and a targeted screen.
directions.question: Truly dark genes with strong phenotypes appear less often in stress conditions than annotation-lag genes (28.7% versus 43.2%) and more often in nutrient, mixed-community and iron conditions. A second stress comparison from the same analysis gives 43.3% versus 54.7%. Does the pattern hold once definitions and condition coverage are aligned?
directions.readiness_basis: The aligned comparison and co-fitness step use existing fitness data; the confirming screens would need new measurements.
directions.test: In the Fitness Browser, restrict to organisms with deep, comparable condition panels (for example Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 with 121 conditions). Within each organism, compute the stress share of strong-phenotype genes for truly dark and annotation-lag genes with one common definition and denominator, so that both reported comparisons can be traced. Then compute co-fitness of strong-phenotype truly dark genes with annotated genes and compare transport and iron-acquisition partners against stress-response partners. For the best candidates, run new fitness screens under iron limitation, alternative nitrogen sources and mixed carbon, and compare phenotype rates with a matched general-stress screen.
directions.title: Do truly dark genes act in nutrient and iron acquisition more than in stress defence?
directions.why_it_matters: Dark genes are ranked for experiments partly as stress-response candidates. If truly dark genes act mostly in acquisition, screens should be built around nutrient and metal shifts. The two analyses compare different groups (all dark genes versus truly dark against annotation-lag), and organisms were tested under different numbers of conditions, so the answer must come from a design that equalises both.

directions.hypothesis: The extra exchange of bridging families is explained by how many distinct domain architectures they have. Families with many architectures are exchanged more regardless of category, and the bridging effect disappears once architecture count is matched.
directions.outcomes: Support: the bridging excess vanishes in architecture-matched comparisons. Refutation: it persists in matched comparisons, pointing to a pathway-level cause, or it fails to reappear on the independent clade subset, in which case the original contrast was probably noise.
directions.prior_work: PMID 16077904 and PMID 37485539 find regulatory and metabolic functions among transferred genes, and PMID 37232518 and PMID 10097118 argue complexity limits transfer. None tests a bridging category against domain architecture.
directions.question: Gene families assigned to both regulatory and metabolic pathways show about twice the rate of cross-lineage exchange of purely regulatory or purely metabolic families (0.57% versus 0.27% and 0.28%), though the differences are small and the observation was exploratory. Is that excess due to many distinct domain combinations, or to bridging pathways being easy to transfer?
directions.readiness_basis: The exchange classification exists, but the architecture census covered only a 376-family subset, so the full census needs compute.
directions.test: For KEGG Orthology families in the Pangenome Collection, tabulate distinct domain architectures, pathway category (regulatory, metabolic, both) and the exchange classification from the gene-transfer atlas. Extend the architecture census beyond the 376-family subset. Compare bridging with single-category families matched for architecture count, and report the rates with uncertainty. Repeat for composite COG assignments such as the mobile-and-defense combination, and test on an independent clade subset not used to find the effect.
directions.title: Do genes bridging regulation and metabolism cross lineages more because of modular domain architecture?
directions.why_it_matters: The complexity hypothesis predicts highly connected genes should transfer less, yet bridging genes appear to transfer more, though by small margins. Because the observation is exploratory, a matched test on independent data would show whether it is real and, if so, whether domain architecture and not pathway membership governs transferability. It also bears on whether multi-category annotations should be filtered out as noise.

directions.hypothesis: Within genera that contain both phaC-positive and phaC-negative species, the positive species come from more variable environments. Accessory phaC occurs mainly in those species, independent of genome size.
directions.outcomes: Support: within genera, phaC-positive species come from more variable environments and carry accessory phaC. Refutation: no environmental difference within genera, or the difference vanishes after genome size and phylogeny are included.
directions.prior_work: PMID 17113245, PMID 24887088 and PMID 33350471 infer transfer of the gene from tree incongruence or islands in individual groups. PMID 42203387 links these storage polymers to fluctuating environments. None combines a within-genus environmental contrast with pangenome class.
directions.question: Phylogenetically discordant carriers of the polyhydroxybutyrate synthase gene phaC keep it in the accessory genome more often (60.1% of 311 species versus 32.3% overall). Does the gene move into lineages that live in more variable environments, or does genome size explain the association?
directions.readiness_basis: The species phaC calls and environment classes exist, but the within-genus design and gene trees have not been built.
directions.test: Using the Pangenome Collection, select genera containing both phaC-positive and phaC-negative species. Compare environmental variability, genome size and phaC pangenome class (core versus accessory) between the two groups within genera. Fit genome size and phylogeny as covariates, and test environmental variability separately inside each genome-size quartile. Compare accessory phaC gene trees with the species tree for incongruence.
directions.title: Is polyhydroxybutyrate storage gained repeatedly by transfer in lineages facing fluctuating environments?
directions.why_it_matters: The apparent link between storage and niche breadth was found to be confounded by genome size, which leaves the feast-and-famine explanation untested. A within-genus design could show whether environmental fluctuation selects for acquiring a storage trait.

directions.hypothesis: Three predictions follow. Raising NDH-2 capacity on a Complex I-deficient background restores growth on quinate. Slowing quinate flux does the same. Deleting NDH-2 makes Complex I required on glucose.
directions.outcomes: Support requires all three: overexpression rescues the Complex I deletion on quinate, slowed quinate uptake reduces the requirement, and NDH-2 deletion makes Complex I required on glucose, with a higher NADH ratio on quinate. Refutation: overexpression leaves the quinate requirement unchanged (against the capacity prediction), slowed uptake leaves it unchanged (against the burst prediction), or NDH-2 deletion leaves glucose growth independent of Complex I. If only some hold, the burst model is incomplete.
directions.prior_work: PMID 18319726 and PMID 25374488 describe ADP1 quinate growth phenotypes and expression changes. PMID 8157582 reports acetate-specific defects in E. coli complex I mutants. None tests whether NADH burst rate sets the Complex I requirement.
directions.question: In Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1, Complex I is more essential on quinate than on glucose or acetate, although quinate yields fewer NADH per carbon (0.57 versus 1.50). Is this because quinate breakdown releases NADH in a concentrated burst that exceeds the capacity of the alternative NADH dehydrogenase (NDH-2)?
directions.readiness_basis: ADP1 has no NDH-2 growth data, and the cross-species check has only 4 organisms without NDH-2.
directions.test: In ADP1, build an NDH-2 deletion and an NDH-2 overexpression strain on a Complex I deletion background. Measure growth and the NADH to NAD+ ratio on quinate, glucose and acetate, and on quinate at lowered uptake rates. First check in the Pangenome Collection and the Fitness Browser whether Complex I dependence on aromatic substrates tracks NDH-2 presence, using more than the 4 organisms without NDH-2 currently available.
directions.title: Does a burst of NADH from quinate breakdown overwhelm the alternative dehydrogenase in Acinetobacter?
directions.why_it_matters: The explanation attributes a carbon-source-specific respiratory requirement to the rate of NADH production and not to its yield. If it holds, respiratory wiring should be read as a flux property, which would affect how metabolic models predict substrate-dependent essentiality. The stoichiometry behind it is theoretical, not measured flux.

directions.hypothesis: Genes lethal when fully deleted but tolerant of transposon insertion carry their insertions mostly near the end of the gene or outside essential protein domains, so a partly functional product remains. Genes with a different pattern of discordance do not.
directions.outcomes: Support: discordant genes show insertions concentrated in tails or non-essential regions, and tail-truncated alleles grow. Refutation: insertions fall throughout the gene and truncations are lethal, which would point to other causes such as differences in conditions or fitness effects short of lethality.
directions.prior_work: PMID 18319726 built the ADP1 complete deletion collection and PMID 25968644 introduced barcoded transposon fitness. Neither explains the disagreement between the two assays gene by gene.
directions.question: In Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 rich medium, why do genes that cannot be fully deleted often tolerate transposon insertions? Is it because partly functional truncated proteins survive?
directions.readiness_basis: The decisive step needs new truncation strains and growth measurements, and insertion-level ADP1 transposon data may also not be loaded in the lakehouse.
directions.test: For the ADP1 genes lethal as complete deletions but dispensable by transposon sequencing, map insertion positions against protein domains and gene ends, and compare with genes where both methods agree. Then build truncation alleles for a handful of these genes, delete the tail or domain, and test whether growth in rich medium survives.
directions.title: Do truncated proteins explain genes lethal when deleted but tolerant of transposon insertion?
directions.why_it_matters: Transposon screens are the standard way to call essential genes across bacteria. If truncation rescue is common, essential gene sets and the minimal-gene-set picture built from them are systematically too small for some gene classes.

directions.hypothesis: Within a single gene, abundance across growth conditions rises when that gene's loss costs more, because cells overproduce proteins whose loss would hurt growth. The genome-wide link between abundance and essentiality is mostly a between-gene effect of housekeeping genes and is weaker within genes.
directions.outcomes: Support: within-gene abundance moves with deletion cost across carbon sources. Refutation: abundance is flat across conditions or unrelated to deletion cost, leaving only the between-gene association.
directions.prior_work: PMID 39253634 reports that most essential A. baylyi proteins are overabundant, but it does not test whether abundance tracks condition-specific cost. PMID 18319726 gives the condition-specific deletion phenotypes needed.
directions.question: Why does average protein abundance across Acinetobacter strains predict which ADP1 genes are essential only fairly well? Does abundance track how strongly a gene is needed in the particular condition?
directions.readiness_basis: Existing proteomics are averages over seven Acinetobacter strains, not ADP1 under matched conditions.
directions.test: Measure ADP1 proteomes on the eight carbon sources already phenotyped in the deletion collection. For each gene, compare abundance across carbon sources with its deletion growth defect on each. Separately compare housekeeping and non-housekeeping genes.
directions.title: Is a protein's abundance a bet on how much its loss would hurt growth?
directions.why_it_matters: If cells tune abundance to the cost of losing a gene, proteomics could rank conditional gene importance without making mutants. If not, the genome-wide link is only a housekeeping correlation.

directions.hypothesis: Most such genes are addiction-type genes, for example toxin-antitoxin or replication-maintenance genes of plasmids and prophages. They become dispensable once the element is removed, and the strain lacks no core function that they replace.
directions.outcomes: Support: neighbourhoods are enriched for mobile-element partners, and curing the element makes the gene dispensable. Refutation: the genes sit in core-like operons, remain essential after the element is removed, and genomes lacking them lack a core function the gene could replace.
directions.prior_work: PMID 33760724 links Xanthomonas essential genes outside the core to mobile elements, and PMID 36097170 shows strain-dependent essentiality in S. pneumoniae. Neither separates addiction from compensation by removing the element.
directions.question: Some genes are essential in the Fitness Browser organism where they were measured yet are accessory across related genomes, and many are poorly annotated or tied to mobile elements. Do they keep cells alive by replacing a missing core function, or because a mobile element makes the cell dependent on them?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness calls and pangenome links exist, but the decisive element-curing step needs new strains and growth measurements.
directions.test: Take the essential-auxiliary genes in Fitness Browser organisms and annotate their neighbourhoods for antitoxins, replication proteins and integrases, and check whether genomes lacking the gene lack the element or lack a core function. Then, for a few genes lying on a plasmid or prophage, cure or delete the element in the host and ask whether the gene stops being essential; compare with essential core genes.
directions.title: Are accessory essential genes mobile-element addictions or stand-ins for missing core functions?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether the loose link between essentiality and core status mostly reflects selfish DNA rather than flexible genome function. That bears on drug-target choice, since accessory essential genes make poor species-wide targets.

directions.hypothesis: Short genes are enriched among recent gains, so length predicts core status through gene age even where insertions are plentiful. Among genes of similar estimated age, length adds little.
directions.outcomes: Support: the length effect vanishes or shrinks within age bins, and age tracks length. Refutation: length keeps predicting core status within age bins and with dense coverage, pointing to a length-linked selection pressure.
directions.prior_work: PMID 38977308 compares orphan and conserved genes on codon use and disorder but not length against core status. PMID 37065130 profiled Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough fitness at scale without testing this.
directions.question: Gene length predicts whether a gene is core better than laboratory fitness does. Is that because short genes are recent arrivals, or only because short genes get fewer transposon insertions?
directions.readiness_basis: Family taxonomic breadth must be computed from cluster membership and is not a ready table.
directions.test: In Fitness Browser organisms linked to the Pangenome Collection, estimate gene age from the taxonomic breadth of each gene's family, using UniRef Clusters membership and pangenome species placement. Fit core status on length, age and insertion density together, and ask whether length still predicts core status among genes with dense insertion coverage and matched age.
directions.title: Does gene length predict core status because short genes are young?
directions.why_it_matters: It separates a real evolutionary pattern, that new genes are short and short-lived, from a measurement artifact. That changes whether fitness data can say anything about conservation.

directions.hypothesis: Shared metal and salt genes reflect osmotic and membrane stress, so they also matter under an equal osmotic load without ions, such as sorbitol, and less so under KCl or choline chloride.
directions.outcomes: Osmotic cause supported: shared genes respond to sorbitol. Ionic cause supported: they respond to KCl or choline chloride but not sorbitol. Sodium-specific cause supported: they respond to NaCl only. Refutation of general stress: shared genes are absent from every control condition.
directions.prior_work: PMID 27474723 and PMID 34432491 profile metal toxicity by transposon fitness. They do not separate osmotic from ionic causes using matched controls.
directions.question: Of the metal-important gene records, 39.8 percent are also important under NaCl stress, and zinc sulfate, which adds no chloride, shows 44.6 percent overlap. Does the overlap come from osmotic load, from sodium or other ion effects, or from shared envelope damage?
directions.readiness_basis: Existing data lack the matched osmotic and potassium controls.
directions.test: In Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough and Pseudomonas stutzeri RCH2, run transposon-library fitness assays under zinc, cobalt and iron alongside NaCl, KCl, sorbitol and choline chloride at matched osmolarity. For the genes shared between metal and NaCl, ask which of the control conditions they also respond to.
directions.title: Is the overlap between metal and salt stress genes ionic or osmotic?
directions.why_it_matters: It would tell which metal-fitness genes are specific metal defences and which are general stress genes, and what a clean metal-specific list needs excluded.

directions.hypothesis: A substantial share of singleton genes confer protection or counter-defence only when phages are present, so they are neutral in standard conditions but matter under phage challenge.
directions.outcomes: Support: singleton genes, mainly phage-related ones, show strong effects under phage challenge but not in standard conditions. Refutation: singletons stay neutral under phage challenge too, favouring lack of function or other niches.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29769716 maps condition-specific phenotypes for poorly annotated genes without phage challenge. PMID 9419362 shows small effects for non-essential yeast genes but does not test hidden conditions.
directions.question: Genes found in one genome show near-zero fitness effects, and condition-specific genes are not more accessory. Are singletons idle, or do they act in conditions the lab never imposes, such as phage attack?
directions.readiness_basis: Predictions use existing data, but phage-challenge fitness has not been measured.
directions.test: Pick Fitness Browser organisms with phages in PhageFoundry Browsers. Predict phage-related singleton genes, run transposon-library fitness under infection, and compare phage-related with other singletons, and with core genes.
directions.title: Are singleton genes neutral in the lab because they act only against phages?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain why laboratory fitness fails to explain the accessory genome and show where hidden function lies. It would also direct fitness screens to phage challenge.

directions.hypothesis: Measuring the ADP1 deletion collection under a broad panel of stress and nitrogen-source conditions will reveal several new discrete modules beyond the quinate aromatic-degradation module. Chemical perturbation across the same carbon sources will not produce more discrete modules than gene deletion does.
directions.outcomes: Support: new conditions yield several discrete, pathway-coherent modules, and chemical perturbation is no more modular than deletion. Refute: ADP1 stays continuous across many added conditions (pointing to organism biology), or chemical perturbation gives clearly sharper modules (pointing to perturbation type).
directions.prior_work: PMID 18319726 built the ADP1 deletion collection and PMID 38323821 found modules in Pseudomonas putida fitness data. Neither measures ADP1 deletions beyond carbon sources or compares deletion with chemical perturbation in the same organism.
directions.question: ADP1 deletion phenotypes on 8 carbon sources form a continuous gradient with one discrete module, yet transposon data from many other bacteria resolve numerous stable modules. Is the gradient caused by testing only carbon sources, by deleting single genes, or by ADP1's own interconnected metabolism?
directions.readiness_basis: The decisive step is new growth measurements on the ADP1 deletion collection and wild-type chemical exposures; only the reference comparison uses existing data.
directions.test: Grow the ADP1 deletion collection under a new panel of oxidative, osmotic, metal and iron-limited stresses plus several nitrogen sources, alongside the original carbon sources. Cluster the new profiles with the same hierarchical method used before and with independent component analysis, and count discrete modules and their pathway content. In parallel, expose wild-type ADP1 to chemical inhibitors across the same carbon sources and compare how discrete the resulting structure is with that from deletions. Compare against module structure in Fitness Browser organisms as a reference.
directions.title: Does ADP1 stay a continuous gradient when probed with stress, nitrogen and chemical perturbations?
directions.why_it_matters: If new condition classes expose hidden modules, a continuous landscape reflects a narrow assay panel and not intrinsic biology. If modules stay absent, perturbation type or ADP1 metabolism sets the architecture, which changes how module calls from any one screen should be read.

directions.hypothesis: Variable essentiality is mostly explained by the dispensable organisms having a paralog or an alternative route that covers the function. Genetic background differences unrelated to redundancy explain little.
directions.outcomes: Support: dispensable organisms consistently carry extra copies or alternative routes, and removing them restores essentiality. Refute: paralog and pathway content do not differ between the groups, and essentiality does not shift after paralog removal.
directions.prior_work: PMID 36097170 and PMID 42726091 describe strain-dependent essential genes within one species or family, and PMID 33753464 shows some ribosomal proteins are dispensable in some lineages. None tests redundancy as the cause across dozens of distant bacteria.
directions.question: Across 48 bacteria, just over a quarter of ortholog families are essential in some organisms and dispensable in others, and a family counted as universally essential only needs to be essential wherever it occurs; only 15 families are essential in all 48 organisms. What makes the same family essential in one genome and dispensable in another?
directions.readiness_basis: Essentiality calls, ortholog families and genome content are in the lakehouse, but the redundancy scoring still has to be built.
directions.test: For variably essential families in the Fitness Browser, compare organisms where the family is essential with those where it is dispensable. Count paralogs in each genome and look for an alternative enzyme covering the same reaction. Use the Pangenome Collection to check whether the same contrast holds across strains within a species. Test the strongest candidates by deleting the paralog in a dispensable organism and checking whether essentiality appears.
directions.title: Are genes essential in some bacteria but not others rescued by redundancy?
directions.why_it_matters: If redundancy explains it, essentiality can be predicted from genome content and the short list essential in every organism becomes a stable core. If not, essentiality depends on hidden organism-specific physiology that gene-content models will miss.

directions.hypothesis: Genes for iron-sulfur cluster assembly and repair, and for iron-sulfur enzymes, account for most of the iron–zinc overlap. Iron supplementation will relieve zinc-sensitive fitness defects in those genes but not in zinc-export genes.
directions.outcomes: Support: iron-sulfur genes dominate the overlap and iron addition rescues their zinc defects selectively. Refute: the overlap is spread across unrelated functions, or iron rescues all zinc defects equally, suggesting general stress.
directions.prior_work: PMID 31586033 shows zinc excess raises iron demand in Escherichia coli, and PMID 37272830 links iron uptake to zinc responses in one species. Neither tests iron-sulfur damage as the shared mechanism across many organisms.
directions.question: Iron and zinc show unexpectedly strong shared gene-level tolerance across organisms. Does zinc toxicity act through iron-sulfur cluster damage?
directions.readiness_basis: The overlap analysis uses existing Fitness Browser data, but the decisive iron-rescue experiment has no existing data.
directions.test: In the Fitness Browser organisms with iron and zinc experiments, split the genes behind the iron–zinc overlap by function. Test whether iron-sulfur assembly, repair and iron-sulfur-containing enzyme genes are over-represented compared with the rest of the overlap. In one tractable organism, run barcoded transposon fitness under zinc with and without added iron.
directions.title: Does zinc excess kill bacteria by damaging iron-sulfur proteins?
directions.why_it_matters: A mechanism for the iron–zinc link would show which cellular targets make metals toxic together. It would also separate chemistry-specific cross-tolerance from a generic stress response, which the metal studies could not do.

directions.hypothesis: The mismatch arises because trace aromatic compounds in nominally aromatic-free media make these genes necessary. Under rigorously scrubbed media the aromatic degradation genes will become dispensable, as the model predicts.
directions.outcomes: Support: defects shrink in scrubbed media and reappear with added trace aromatics, matching the revised model. Refute: defects stay unchanged without any aromatic source, pointing to a real requirement or a regulatory effect the model omits.
directions.prior_work: PMID 18840283 used ADP1 knockout data to refine a metabolic model, and PMID 18319726 phenotyped the deletion collection. Neither tests whether trace media components cause the aromatic-pathway discrepancies.
directions.question: In ADP1, flux balance predictions and transposon essentiality disagree for about a quarter of shared genes, and aromatic degradation genes are strongly enriched among them. Is the mismatch a missing model input or a real substrate requirement?
directions.readiness_basis: The ADP1 deletion collection, existing growth data and model exist, but the decisive growth assays in purified media do not.
directions.test: Regrow ADP1 deletion mutants of the 24 quinate-specific aromatic degradation genes in carefully purified defined media, with and without a defined trace of aromatic substrates. Compare growth with the existing ADP1 deletion growth data and with flux balance predictions made with the same media composition in the ModelSEED Biochemistry framework.
directions.title: Do trace aromatics in growth media explain model mismatches for aromatic degradation genes?
directions.why_it_matters: If trace inputs cause the mismatch, discordant genes can be partly resolved by correcting media rather than rewriting metabolism, and the sole discrete phenotypic module would reflect environmental contamination. If not, the model lacks real biology.

directions.hypothesis: Efflux pump mutants will be more sensitive to antibiotics when histidine or tryptophan is limiting, and amino acid supplementation will reduce that sensitivity. Other resistance mechanisms will not respond this way.
directions.outcomes: Support: efflux gene fitness shifts with amino acid supplementation under antibiotic, while other mechanism classes do not. Refute: supplementation changes nothing for efflux genes, or changes all gene classes equally.
directions.prior_work: PMID 21645016 and PMID 39038993 link metabolism and tryptophan transport to antibiotic resistance. They do not test whether efflux dependence changes with amino acid biosynthesis status.
directions.question: Efflux resistance genes neighbor histidine and tryptophan biosynthesis genes in fitness-correlation networks across several organisms, although no function was specific to a resistance mechanism once corrected for repeated testing. Does biosynthesis status modulate efflux dependence?
directions.readiness_basis: Antibiotic and standard-condition fitness data exist, but the supplementation contrast needs new experiments.
directions.test: In a Fitness Browser organism with many efflux genes, run barcoded transposon fitness under a sub-inhibitory antibiotic with and without histidine and tryptophan supplementation. Compare efflux, enzymatic-inactivation and metal-resistance genes. Use existing Fitness Browser data to check whether the histidine and tryptophan biosynthesis neighborhoods are stronger under antibiotics than in standard growth.
directions.title: Does amino acid biosynthesis shape how much efflux pumps matter for antibiotic tolerance?
directions.why_it_matters: A metabolic dependence of efflux-mediated tolerance would show that nutrient state changes drug susceptibility, so culture medium choice would matter for resistance testing. A null result would support the view that this enrichment only reflects genes being dispensable in the lab.

directions.hypothesis: Resistance genes that are core are those whose products also serve non-antibiotic roles, such as envelope maintenance or stress handling. Within a mechanism class they should show fitness effects under non-antibiotic stresses and co-vary with non-resistance genes, whereas accessory ones should be functionally isolated.
directions.outcomes: Support: core resistance genes show more non-antibiotic phenotypes and stronger co-variation with envelope or regulatory genes than accessory ones of the same mechanism. Refute: the two groups look alike once mechanism is held fixed, which would point to mobility rather than physiological integration.
directions.prior_work: PMID 35873140 shows some efflux genes are core in one species and PMID 25861385 shows cost varies by drug class, but neither asks what non-antibiotic role could make a resistance gene permanent.
directions.question: Resistance mechanism strongly predicts whether a resistance gene is core or accessory, yet it does not predict knockout fitness cost. Intrinsic efflux pumps such as emhABC are more than 95% core, beta-lactamases are 54.9% core, regulatory genes are 6.5% core, and blaTEM, tet(C) and ant(2'')-Ia are 0% core. What besides cost explains this spread?
directions.readiness_basis: Resistance genes were already linked to fitness data and core status across 25 organisms, so the first step uses existing linked tables; the knockout step needs new measurements.
directions.test: The mechanism labels came from keyword matching on product descriptions, so first re-assign them from the gene annotations and check that the core-versus-accessory spread survives. Then, for resistance genes in Fitness Browser organisms with conservation status from the Pangenome Collection, compare core and accessory genes within each mechanism class. Measure (a) fitness under non-antibiotic stresses such as detergents, osmotic stress and metals, and (b) how closely each gene's fitness pattern tracks that of non-resistance genes across all experiments. Then knock out a core efflux operon such as emhABC in a host that carries it and test growth under envelope stress.
directions.title: Is a resistance gene's conservation set by how embedded it is in physiology?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate resistance genes that are permanent parts of cell physiology from true add-ons. That changes which resistance genes can be targeted without side effects, and explains conservation without invoking cost.

directions.hypothesis: Resistance genes whose base and codon composition differs most from their host genome, an indirect hint of more recent acquisition, carry the highest cost, and cost shrinks as composition becomes host-like and prevalence within a species rises.
directions.outcomes: Support: cost falls steadily as composition becomes host-like, independent of singleton status. Refute: cost is flat across the composition gradient, or the singleton signal disappears when one gene-linking method is used for all classes.
directions.prior_work: PMID 25861385 and PMID 29439838 describe cost and compensation for resistance mutations, but they do not test whether the cost of native resistance genes decays with time since acquisition in genome-wide knockout data.
directions.question: Core and accessory resistance genes have identical baseline knockout fitness, yet a separate analysis finds that single-genome resistance genes are the costliest class. Is cost tied to how recently a gene arrived rather than to its core or accessory label?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene linking and fitness exist, but composition-deviation metrics must be computed from genome sequences.
directions.test: In Fitness Browser organisms with linked pangenomes, take each resistance gene's sequence from KBase Genomes and compute its deviation in base composition and codon usage from the host genome, together with within-species prevalence from the Pangenome Collection. Composition deviation is only a proxy and does not give acquisition history, so also check whether it separates singleton genes from widely shared ones. Ask whether baseline knockout fitness is predicted by the deviation among non-singleton genes as well as singletons. For a strain carrying a likely recent acquisition, run a competition assay between carrier and knockout strain without antibiotic.
directions.title: Do newly acquired resistance genes pay a cost that fades as they are integrated?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, cost is transient after acquisition, and the absent core-versus-accessory difference hides a time-dependent cost. That would help explain how resistance persists once acquired.

directions.hypothesis: Many of its costly dispensable genes are costly only in aerobic growth. They should lose their cost under anaerobic denitrifying conditions and be less rich in mobile-element annotations than the costly genes that stay costly.
directions.outcomes: Support: a large share of the costly set loses its cost anaerobically and is not mobile-element rich. Refute: cost persists across oxygen states and stays concentrated in transposase, phage and insertion-sequence genes, which favours genomic invasion.
directions.prior_work: PMID 32994326 shows gene dispensability depends on carbon environment in E. coli, and PMID 22448042 predicts loss of costly dispensable functions, but neither tests whether an outlier organism's costly set is an assay-mismatch effect.
directions.question: About a fifth of the genes in Pseudomonas stutzeri RCH2 (21.5%) are costly in the lab yet dispensable, far above the next organism (14.0%). Are they costly only because the lab differs from this denitrifier's natural anaerobic life, or do they reflect accumulation of costly mobile DNA?
directions.readiness_basis: The existing oxygen comparison in RCH2 is confounded with metal salt, so the decisive matched aerobic and anaerobic competition has to be newly measured.
directions.test: Existing aerobic and anaerobic experiments in RCH2 are confounded with the metal salt used, so they can only frame the question. Use the Fitness Browser to list RCH2's costly dispensable genes and compare mobile-element keyword enrichment and singleton share against the other costly genes. The decisive step is new: run pooled mutant competition in a defined medium under aerobic and anaerobic nitrate-reducing growth with no metal added, and see which genes change cost.
directions.title: Is one denitrifier's costly dispensable gene set a lab mismatch or mobile-DNA load?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether outlier organisms in cost surveys reveal real genomic parasitism or only a mismatch between assay and native lifestyle, which affects how lab-cost results are read as evidence for selection in nature.

directions.hypothesis: Metabolic ecotypes predict isolation environment better than core-genome subclade membership alone does, and pathways that vary within a species are those tied to nutrient sources of different habitats.
directions.outcomes: Support: ecotype labels carry environment information beyond what subclade labels carry, concentrated in nutrient-use pathways. Refute: environment is explained by subclade, or ecotype and environment are unrelated across species.
directions.prior_work: PMID 24465487 links metabolic flexibility to spatial distribution of communities and PMID 22928415 maps soil niche space by traits, but neither tests ecotypes inside species against isolation environment with phylogeny held fixed.
directions.question: Species with many genomes split into a handful of metabolic ecotypes by their pathway profiles. Do these ecotypes correspond to distinct isolation environments, or do they simply mirror subclades?
directions.readiness_basis: Pathway profiles and isolation metadata exist, but subclade structure and metadata harmonisation must be computed, and only a minority of genomes carry environmental embeddings.
directions.test: For the species with at least 50 genomes and variable pathways, cluster genomes by pathway profile in the Pangenome Collection. Score isolation-source categories using genome metadata, supplemented by NMDC BioSamples where strains link. Compare how well ecotype labels and core-genome subclade labels each predict isolation category within species, and whether the discriminating pathways are carbon or nitrogen utilization routes.
directions.title: Do the metabolic ecotypes within a bacterial species track where its strains live?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that within-species metabolic variation is ecological adaptation rather than neutral drift, and give a way to infer habitat from genome content. The planned niche-breadth test for these ecotypes was never run.

directions.hypothesis: Metal-important genes involved in uptake, cofactor biosynthesis or metal-dependent enzymes are strongly core, while detoxification and efflux genes for metals with no biological role are much less core, so the pooled enrichment is a mixture of the two.
directions.outcomes: Support: uptake and cofactor genes are clearly more core than detoxification genes, and the difference between metal classes shrinks after the split. Refute: both gene types are similarly core, or toxic-only metals are as core-enriched as essential metals.
directions.prior_work: PMID 34765088 reports that most cadmium-responsive genes in one Enterococcus faecium strain are core, and PMID 34432491 and PMID 40302248 map metal-tolerance genes, but none separates essential-metal handling from toxicity defense when asking about conservation.
directions.question: Removing genes also important under salt stress left core-genome enrichment of metal-important genes intact, and strengthened it for essential metals; cadmium and iron, each in one organism, moved the other way. Do essential-metal use and acquisition genes carry the enrichment, while toxic-metal defense genes are as variable as other accessory genes?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness data and core status already exist, but gene function labels must be assigned and the cadmium and iron results rest on one organism each.
directions.test: In Fitness Browser organisms with metal experiments, label each metal-important gene by annotation as uptake or cofactor use versus detoxification or efflux. Compare core fractions from the Pangenome Collection for each label, for essential metals (molybdenum, tungsten, selenium, nickel) versus toxic-only metals (mercury, cadmium, uranium), after removing genes also important under salt stress. Repeat with organisms contributing more than one metal to see whether the split holds within a genome.
directions.title: Does essential-metal cofactor handling, not toxicity defense, drive core enrichment of metal-fitness genes?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain why different analyses disagree about whether metal genes are core or accessory, and show that conservation of metal fitness genes reflects ordinary physiology rather than adaptation to contaminated sites.

directions.hypothesis: Within genera that contain both soil/sediment and non-soil genomes, soil-derived genomes carry xoxF more often than their non-soil relatives, and inferred gain events fall more often on soil branches.
directions.outcomes: Support: a consistent soil excess within genera across several phyla, with gains concentrated on soil branches. Refutation: the excess disappears within genera, or appears in only one or two lineages, which points to lineage composition.
directions.prior_work: PMID 38369453 found xoxF gene clusters in Acidobacteria and other phyla from weathered granite and soil but did not test habitat against lineage; this asks whether habitat is associated with xoxF within lineages.
directions.question: Does the soil and sediment excess of xoxF persist when only close relatives are compared, so that it cannot be explained by which lineages happen to live in soil?
directions.readiness_basis: Genome and habitat data are in the lakehouse, but the within-genus tree building and gain/loss reconstruction need new computation.
directions.test: In the Pangenome Collection, take genera with genomes from both soil/sediment and other habitats, using habitat labels from NMDC BioSamples where available. Compare xoxF carriage between habitats within each genus. Build genus trees and reconstruct gain and loss to see whether gains map to soil branches. Repeat in several xoxF-carrying phyla, including Acidobacteriota, where the enrichment already survived a within-phylum comparison. Use annotations from both sources, since they disagree for xoxF. This is observational and can show association only. Selection would need a follow-up, such as lanthanide-limited growth of soil and non-soil relatives.
directions.title: Is soil habitat associated with xoxF gain inside single lineages, beyond lineage makeup?
directions.why_it_matters: A within-genus association would show that the soil signal is not only a by-product of methylotroph-rich lineages living in soil, and would justify testing selection directly. It would also show whether xoxF can serve as a habitat marker.

directions.hypothesis: Lanmodulin-positive genomes with xoxF confirmed absent carry other lanthanide-linked functions (for example other PQQ alcohol dehydrogenases) or come from lanthanide-rich habitats, so lanmodulin is retained for lanthanide handling independent of methanol oxidation.
directions.outcomes: Support: confirmed xoxF-free genomes consistently carry another lanthanide-linked enzyme or come from lanthanide-rich sources, and the deletion changes lanthanide-dependent growth or uptake. Refutation: xoxF is found in nearly all of them once better searches are used, or they carry no other partner, so lanmodulin simply tracks xoxF.
directions.prior_work: PMID 30351021 and 35814700 characterise lanmodulin in Methylobacterium and tie it to the lanthanide methanol dehydrogenase; PMID 41023737 surveys the lanthanome in methane oxidisers. None asks what lanmodulin does where xoxF is truly missing.
directions.question: Among lanmodulin-carrying genomes, those lacking an xoxF call may truly lack it or may reflect incomplete annotation. If sequence-level checks confirm xoxF is absent, do these genomes use lanthanides in other enzymes, or for storage or detoxification?
directions.readiness_basis: The genomic screen is feasible now, but the function test needs growth and metal-uptake work in a lanmodulin-positive, xoxF-free strain.
directions.test: Take the lanmodulin-positive genomes in Beijerinckiaceae, Acetobacteraceae and Hyphomicrobiaceae and flag those without an xoxF call from either annotation source. Confirm absence with a sequence-profile search for XoxF clades and an assembly completeness check, and keep only confirmed-absent genomes. Search that group in UniProt Annotations and UniRef Clusters for other PQQ-dependent dehydrogenases and for genes neighbouring lanmodulin, and compare isolation sources. Then, in one confirmed xoxF-free strain, grow with and without lanthanum and delete lanmodulin to see whether growth or metal uptake changes.
directions.title: What do lanmodulin-carrying bacteria without a confirmed xoxF use lanthanides for?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate lanthanide handling from methanol oxidation and show a wider role for lanthanides in bacteria than the methylotroph picture suggests. If xoxF turns out to be present, lanmodulin simply tracks it.

directions.hypothesis: The lanmodulin gene tree disagrees with the species tree, and the gene sits next to mobile-element or insertion-like genes in some genomes, which points to horizontal transfer.
directions.outcomes: Support: clear gene-tree/species-tree conflict, copies in mobile-associated contexts, and base composition unlike the host. Refutation: the gene tree follows the species tree and the neighbourhood is conserved, which means vertical inheritance with lineage-specific loss.
directions.prior_work: PMID 30351021, 35814700 and 37259003 characterise single lanmodulins; none reconstructs how the gene moved among lineages.
directions.question: Lanmodulin occurs only in three alpha-Proteobacterial methylotroph families. Was it inherited from a common ancestor and lost elsewhere, or passed sideways between lineages that share habitats?
directions.readiness_basis: Genome and annotation data are present; tree building and synteny comparison need new computation.
directions.test: Using the Pangenome Collection, build a gene tree for lanmodulin proteins from the bakta-validated genomes and compare it with the species tree. Test whether closely related species differ in carrying lanmodulin. Check the flanking genes of each copy for transposases, integrases and phage genes, and compare the base composition of the gene with its host genome.
directions.title: Was lanmodulin spread by horizontal transfer among alpha-Proteobacterial methylotrophs?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain the narrow distribution and show whether metal-handling proteins move between lineages in the same habitat, which bears on how lanthanide use evolves.

directions.hypothesis: A large share of xoxF carriers across phyla lack the downstream one-carbon pathways needed to use methanol, so the xoxF-over-mxaF excess reflects broad alcohol oxidation, not methylotrophy.
directions.outcomes: Support: many carriers lack the downstream route and the enzyme prefers longer alcohols. Refutation: nearly all carriers have a complete one-carbon route and the enzyme is most active on methanol.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29404411 and 26858104 show xoxF as the main methanol dehydrogenase in particular methylotrophs and PMID 41636527 reviews wider methylotrophic metabolism; this tests whether the genome-wide excess is methanol-related at all.
directions.question: If xoxF outnumbers mxaF so strongly, do most carriers actually run a full methanol-to-formaldehyde-to-energy route, or does xoxF mainly act on other alcohols or aldehydes in bacteria that are not methylotrophs?
directions.readiness_basis: The genome classification can be done on lakehouse data, but substrate preference requires enzyme assays.
directions.test: In the Pangenome Collection, classify xoxF-carrying genomes by presence of formaldehyde-oxidation and one-carbon assimilation genes, per phylum and with both annotation sources combined. Then, for non-methylotroph carriers in soil lineages such as Acidobacteriota, measure enzyme activity of purified XoxF against methanol, ethanol and other alcohols with and without lanthanides.
directions.title: Is xoxF mostly a methanol enzyme, or does it serve other alcohols in non-methylotrophs?
directions.why_it_matters: It would redefine the xoxF count as a measure of lanthanide-dependent alcohol chemistry, and change how xoxF abundance in soils and wetlands is read as methanol cycling.

directions.hypothesis: Lanthanide-dependent methylotrophs are enriched at lanthanide-rich sites of near-neutral pH but not in acidic, metal-laden drainage, where stress genes dominate.
directions.outcomes: Support: xoxF enrichment at neutral rare-earth-rich sites but not acidic ones, and lanthanum-stimulated enrichments only at neutral pH. Refutation: acidic sites are equally enriched, or neutral rare-earth sites show no excess over matched controls.
directions.prior_work: PMID 33848048 describes the microbiota of a river hit by rare-earth mining drainage, and PMID 38369453 finds lanthanide enzymes in weathered granite and soil; neither compares sites by acidity to see what gates lanthanide-dependent organisms.
directions.question: Acid-mine-drainage genomes from a rare-earth mining site carried little xoxF and no lanmodulin. Does acid and metal stress override lanthanide availability, so that xoxF enrichment appears only at rare-earth-rich sites with milder chemistry?
directions.readiness_basis: The earlier rare-earth set was small and from a single project, so more metagenomes or new enrichments are needed.
directions.test: Search NMDC Multi-omics and NMDC BioSamples for metagenomes from rare-earth-rich soils, weathered rock, mine tailings and acid drainage, plus matched non-rare-earth controls, and compare xoxF and lanmodulin carriage and stress-gene profiles by pH class. Then run methanol enrichments of neutral and acidic rare-earth-rich material with and without added lanthanum, and measure xoxF expression and lanthanide uptake.
directions.title: Do rare-earth-rich sites select lanthanide-dependent methylotrophs only when acidity does not dominate?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that lanthanide supply alone does not recruit lanthanide-dependent organisms and that pH or co-occurring metals gate it. This sets where to look for them in rare-earth mining and recovery settings.

directions.hypothesis: Acid-drainage genomes from rare-earth sites carry lanthanide-binding proteins with calcium-binding-like motifs but no match to known families, and these bind lanthanides more strongly than calcium.
directions.outcomes: Support: candidates enriched at the rare-earth site over the control that bind lanthanides preferentially. Refutation: candidates are equally common in the control or bind calcium as well as lanthanides.
directions.prior_work: PMID 34432449 and 37259003 characterise lanmodulin binding; this searches for binders that annotation-based detection could not find.
directions.question: With no lanmodulin or xoxF in most acid-drainage genomes from the rare-earth site, do those organisms handle lanthanides with proteins that annotation cannot recognise?
directions.readiness_basis: Motif scanning needs new computation and the binding test needs protein expression and spectroscopy.
directions.test: Scan the acid-drainage genomes for proteins with lanmodulin-like or calcium-binding motif patterns and predicted secreted or periplasmic location, excluding those with annotated homologs. Compare their frequency with matched genomes from acid drainage without rare earths. Express the top candidates and test lanthanide and calcium binding by sensitised terbium luminescence.
directions.title: Do rare-earth-rich acid sites use lanthanide-binding proteins unrelated to known ones?
directions.why_it_matters: It would reveal lanthanide-handling systems outside the known protein families and show that gene annotation missed them. It could also give new proteins for rare-earth recovery.

directions.hypothesis: Desulfovibrio vulgaris grows without added serine by making it from glycine and one-carbon units through a non-canonical route, so the predicted gap is a blind spot in the predictor and not an auxotrophy.
directions.outcomes: Growth and labelled serine without added serine, plus a fitness cost for the glycine-to-serine gene, would support a missed route. No growth without serine, and no fitness cost for any candidate gene, would support a true auxotrophy and refute the hypothesis.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29324779 used high-throughput genetics to fill amino acid pathway gaps predicted by automated tools, and PMID 15077118 gives the genome; neither says whether this organism makes serine without a canonical pathway.
directions.question: Is the lack of a complete serine biosynthesis pathway in Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough a real serine requirement, or does the organism make serine through a route the pathway predictor does not recognise?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness data and pathway calls are in the lakehouse, but the growth and isotope-tracing experiment has not been done.
directions.test: Grow Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough in defined serine-free medium with and without glycine and a one-carbon source. Trace labelled glycine into serine. In parallel, read mutant fitness for the serine hydroxymethyltransferase gene and for any partial serine pathway genes in the Fitness Browser, and compare with the other six organisms that have complete calls.
directions.title: Does Desulfovibrio vulgaris make serine by a route that pathway predictors miss?
directions.why_it_matters: The organism was the only one of seven with no complete serine pathway call, and the remaining diversity in amino acid pathways was read as ecological adaptation. If the gap is a missed route, that reading is weaker and pathway predictors have a systematic blind spot in sulfate reducers. If it is real, it is a rare natural serine auxotrophy.

directions.hypothesis: ACIAD3522 is a flavin-dependent enzyme of acetate catabolism, not a respiratory dehydrogenase, and Complex I subunit defects in ADP1 are as strong on acetate and succinate as on quinate.
directions.outcomes: Deletions with a defect only on acetate and a rescue by a downstream intermediate would support a catabolic role. Equal Complex I defects across all four substrates would refute an aromatic-specific bottleneck. Defects confined to quinate would support the flux reading and refute the hypothesis.
directions.prior_work: PMID 18319726 provides the deletion collection and PMID 18840283 the metabolic model; neither tests whether elevated modelled respiratory flux predicts condition-specific essentiality.
directions.question: In Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1, is the gene ACIAD3522 needed for acetate growth because it works in respiratory NADH oxidation, or because it acts in acetate catabolism itself, and is Complex I's aromatic requirement real in ADP1?
directions.readiness_basis: Deletion mutants exist in the published ADP1 collection but growth, redox and rescue data on these substrates are not in the lakehouse.
directions.test: Use the ADP1 single-gene deletion collection to measure growth of the ACIAD3522 deletion and several Complex I subunit deletions on acetate, succinate, quinate and glucose. Add a deletion of a type 2 NADH dehydrogenase if one is found in the genome. Measure NADH to NAD+ balance and test whether acetate-grown deletion strains can be rescued by supplying a downstream intermediate.
directions.title: Is the acetate-specific defect of ACIAD3522 a respiratory role or an acetate catabolism role?
