directions.why_it_matters: Higher modelled Complex I flux on aromatics was read as an aromatic-specific bottleneck, while ortholog-transferred defects were strongest on non-aromatic substrates. Settling this decides whether model flux can point to condition-specific essential genes. It would also give a function to a gene the model routes no flux through.

directions.hypothesis: Most unresolved EC-less reactions are catalysed by members of characterised enzyme families acting on a similar substrate, and the matching carbon-source fitness phenotypes point to those family members.
directions.outcomes: Candidate-family genes enriched for fitness defects on the matching carbon source, and activity in vitro, would support promiscuity. No enrichment over random genes, and no activity, would favour unknown families.
directions.prior_work: PMID 30910961 annotates orphan reactions from reactive-site knowledge and PMID 25968644 supplies the fitness method; neither checks predictions against matched-substrate fitness for gapfilled reactions across many organisms.
directions.question: Why were only a minority of gapfilled reactions with no EC number resolved to a gene, compared with most reactions that have one: are their enzymes unknown families, or known families acting on unusual substrates?
directions.readiness_basis: Reactions, fitness data and annotations are in the lakehouse, but the similarity search over reactions needs new computation.
directions.test: For the 50 EC-less reactions, use reactive-site similarity in ModelSEED Biochemistry to find the nearest EC-bearing reactions and predict candidate families. Check whether genes of those families in the same organism show fitness defects on the matching carbon source more often than randomly chosen genes of similar family size. Test the best candidates in vitro.
directions.title: Are gapfilled reactions without EC numbers carried by promiscuous enzymes of known families?
directions.why_it_matters: Over half of gapfilled pairs lack a convincing gene candidate, so many models carry reactions with no known enzyme. If promiscuity explains them, annotation can use substrate similarity and existing families. If not, they point to new enzyme families needing discovery.

directions.hypothesis: Within soil, community completeness for carbon-use pathways such as cellobiose, galactose and glucuronate rises with the ambient intensity of the matching substrate, and this holds in more than one independent study, because catabolism is retained where the substrate is available.
directions.outcomes: Positive correlations for most carbon pathways in the dominant study and in at least one independent study would support the hypothesis. Absent or negative correlations in the dominant study would refute it. A pattern seen only in the dominant study would leave generality open and would not count as support.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 35085485 and 31316056 link community gene content to metabolite dynamics, and PMID 33311510 treats environmental metabolomes; none contrasts carbon-use and amino acid pathways against ambient substrate levels.
directions.question: Soil communities have broadly higher carbon-use pathway completeness than freshwater ones. Within soil, does completeness for each carbon pathway rise with the ambient level of its own substrate, the opposite of the mostly negative trend seen for amino acid biosynthesis?
directions.readiness_basis: Paired data exist for these samples, but 125 of 131 come from a single study and abiotic data are missing, so testing generality likely requires metabolomics from other studies.
directions.test: Step 1: count how many NMDC studies have paired taxonomy and metabolomics for soil; in the amino acid analysis 125 of 131 samples, and all 62 leucine samples, came from one study, and the 33 freshwater samples had no paired metabolomics. Step 2: compute community completeness for each carbon-use pathway from species-level pathway calls in the Pangenome Collection and correlate it with the matching metabolite intensity within each study separately, alongside amino acid pathways in the same samples. A result from the dominant study alone cannot show generality. Step 3: if fewer than two studies have paired data, generate metabolomics for soils from other studies or for the freshwater samples.
directions.title: Does soil carbon-pathway completeness rise with substrate level, unlike amino acid pathways?
directions.why_it_matters: A split between catabolic genes kept where substrate is supplied and biosynthetic genes lost where product is supplied would give a general rule linking habitat chemistry to community metabolic configuration. A missing or reversed pattern would mean the soil-freshwater carbon difference reflects which taxa live there, not substrate supply. The amino acid result it is contrasted with rests on one study: 125 of 131 samples, including all 62 leucine samples, came from a single NMDC study, so generality beyond it is untested.

directions.hypothesis: Within P. aeruginosa, the sorbitol, mannitol and gluconate pathways were lost several independent times on lung-associated branches, more often than on matched non-lung branches. This is a separate pattern from the group-wide predicted absence of xylose, arabinose and myo-inositol pathways.
directions.outcomes: Support: losses fall repeatedly on separate lung branches, and CF isolates grow worse than environmental isolates on the three sugars. Refutation: the lower scores trace to a few deep lineages that happen to be over-sampled in the lung, or growth does not differ by isolate source.
directions.prior_work: PMID 25409940 and PMID 31214142 show that individual CF isolates use particular substrates differently, and PMID 29607620 and PMID 3922954 describe sugar handling in Pseudomonas. None asks whether loss is repeated within lung lineages as opposed to inherited from the wider group.
directions.question: Is the weaker predicted sugar catabolism of lung and cystic fibrosis P. aeruginosa genomes a set of repeated losses inside the species, or does it only reflect the difference that already separates the P. aeruginosa group from the P. fluorescens group?
directions.readiness_basis: The genome-level analysis uses existing pathway scores, but growth on the sugars needs new isolate assays.
directions.test: Using the Pangenome Collection, place the P. aeruginosa genomes on a within-species tree. Infer on which branches each of the seven lower-scoring carbon pathways changed from complete to incomplete. Ask whether such changes fall on lung-isolate branches more than on matched non-lung branches, and whether they recur in separate lineages. Then grow CF-derived and environmental P. aeruginosa isolates on sorbitol, mannitol and gluconate. Include xylose as a check on the genome-based prediction of absence: if some isolates do grow on it, the predicted absence is wrong for them and the check shows how far the pathway scores can be trusted.
directions.title: Were sugar pathways lost repeatedly within lung-adapted Pseudomonas aeruginosa, independent of deeper lineage differences?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate adaptation to the lung from inherited lineage history. It would also show which sugars a cystic fibrosis airway formulation can count on the pathogen being unable to use.

directions.hypothesis: Within a species, pathways classed as latent are missing from a larger fraction of genomes than active pathways of the same organism. Carbon-utilization pathways, which are more often latent than amino acid pathways, show the most within-species loss.
directions.outcomes: Support: latent pathways are absent from more conspecific genomes than active ones, and the effect is largest for carbon pathways. Refutation: latent and active pathways are equally conserved across strains, so latency reflects limited laboratory conditions rather than relaxed selection.
directions.prior_work: PMID 24910088 and PMID 35575545 treat biosynthetic gene loss in experiments and theory, and PMID 40568968 shows cross-feeding dependence arising in culture. None tests whether laboratory-latent pathways are the ones that vary across strains in natural populations.
directions.question: Do pathways that are genomically complete but show no fitness importance in the laboratory vary more across strains of the same species than pathways that are fitness-important, and does this account for the link between latent pathways and open pangenomes?
directions.readiness_basis: Latent and active labels and per-genome pathway completeness already exist for the organisms involved.
directions.test: For the Fitness Browser organisms already classified as latent or active, use the Pangenome Collection to compute, for each pathway, the fraction of genomes of the same species that carry it complete. Compare latent against active pathways within the same organism, separately for carbon and amino acid pathways. Also ask whether species with more latent pathways have more strain-to-strain variable pathways.
directions.title: Are latent biosynthetic and catabolic pathways the ones lost first within species?
directions.why_it_matters: It would turn a laboratory classification into a testable signature of ongoing gene loss and give the Black Queen idea at species scale a prediction that can fail. The pathway-level conservation comparison found no difference, so this is the first check of loss across strains.

directions.hypothesis: Members of the Brevundimonas-Caulobacter-Sphingomonas cluster can grow at acidic pH when alone but are outcompeted there by the Rhodanobacter cluster. Both clusters tolerate the range between their habitat peaks.
directions.outcomes: Support: monoculture ranges overlap broadly, but in co-culture one cluster is displaced at acidic pH. Refutation: monoculture growth already fails outside each cluster's habitat range, so tolerance alone explains the split.
directions.prior_work: PMID 38366921 and PMID 40118314 link temperature and pH to Ralstonia and Sphingomonas abundance in fish skin and acid mine drainage. They do not test whether a niche split between these clusters reflects tolerance or competition.
directions.question: Do Rhodanobacter, Ralstonia and Dyella occupy more acidic, warmer habitats worldwide than Brevundimonas, Caulobacter and Sphingomonas because of their own tolerance limits, or because each cluster excludes the other where their tolerances overlap?
directions.readiness_basis: Isolates and habitat metadata exist, but growth across pH in monoculture and co-culture has not been measured.
directions.test: Using ENIGMA CORAL isolates and the NMDC BioSamples, select Oak Ridge isolates from both clusters. Measure monoculture growth across a pH series spanning the acidic and neutral habitat means, then co-culture pairs across the same series and track relative abundance by sequencing. Check whether sample-level exclusion of the clusters in NMDC BioSamples peaks at intermediate pH where monocultures overlap.
directions.title: Is the acid and warmth niche split between two Oak Ridge genus clusters caused by competition?
directions.why_it_matters: A tolerance limit and competitive exclusion predict different outcomes for contaminated, acidified aquifers. It would also show whether the global co-occurrence map reflects physiology or interaction.

directions.hypothesis: Co-carriage is rarer than the lineage structure of Burkholderiales alone predicts. Generalist isolates grow more slowly on a single substrate, such as phenylethylamine, than same-genus specialists do on that same substrate, and they use a mixture one substrate at a time rather than together.
directions.outcomes: Support: co-carriage falls below the genus-shuffled expectation, generalists grow more slowly than same-genus specialists on the same single substrate, and mixture use is sequential. Refutation: co-carriage matches the genus null and generalists match specialists on each shared substrate, so any difference is strain identity rather than a burden of co-carriage.
directions.prior_work: PMID 22026719 reports that aromatic catabolic versatility in Burkholderiales is shaped by lineage and habitat. It does not ask whether combining aromatic and non-aromatic capacities is disfavoured or slows growth, which neither PMID 17030797 nor PMID 30811107 tests.
directions.question: Why do only a few genomes carry both an aromatic-compound capacity and a non-aromatic one, and does holding both capacities slow growth on each substrate compared with relatives that hold only one?
directions.readiness_basis: The capacity calls over 3109 genomes exist, but growth of generalist and matched specialist isolates on shared single substrates needs new assays.
directions.test: Within the Pangenome Collection genomes that carry at least one census capacity, compare how often aromatic and non-aromatic capacities co-occur against a null that shuffles capacities among genomes of the same genus. Then pick generalists (Paraburkholderia, Burkholderia, Hydrogenophaga) and single-capacity specialists from the same genera. Grow all of them on the same single substrates: phenylethylamine alone and a non-aromatic substrate alone, so substrate is held fixed and only the number of capacities differs. Also grow the generalists on the mixture and record whether the two substrates are used together or in sequence.
directions.title: Does carrying both aromatic and non-aromatic carbon capacities slow growth on either substrate?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain why versatility looks like a clade trait rather than a portable module. It would also indicate whether engineering aromatic degraders into other chassis carries a hidden growth cost.

directions.hypothesis: Phyla without phaC retain glycogen, polyphosphate or lipid storage at rates similar to PHB-carrying phyla. The absence reflects substitution rather than loss of storage, except in genome-reduced phyla such as Patescibacteria.
directions.outcomes: Support: PHB-absent phyla show alternative storage in most species, with a rate comparable to PHB-carrying phyla. Refutation: PHB-absent phyla also lack the alternatives, especially among small genomes, which points to storage loss tied to genome reduction.
directions.prior_work: PMID 31151997 surveys energy-reserve pathways across 8282 bacterial proteomes and links reserve loss to genome reduction. It does not ask, phylum by phylum, whether a missing PHB pathway is replaced by another reserve in genome-based species sets that include metagenome-assembled genomes.
directions.question: Are phyla with no detected PHB, such as Campylobacterota, Gemmatimonadota, Nanoarchaeota and Marinisomatota, lacking storage altogether, or have they substituted another reserve such as glycogen or polyphosphate?
directions.readiness_basis: Phylum-level phaC counts exist, and alternative storage genes can be searched in the same pangenome annotations.
directions.test: In the Pangenome Collection, score the storage pathways for glycogen, polyphosphate and neutral lipid across species of the PHB-absent phyla and PHB-rich phyla. Compare the share of species with any storage pathway, and test whether PHB absence goes with presence of an alternative pathway after accounting for genome size.
directions.title: Do phyla without PHB carry other carbon-storage systems instead?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether feast-and-famine lifestyles select for storage in general or for PHB in particular. It would also show whether PHB absence in these phyla marks genome reduction or a different strategy.

directions.hypothesis: The glycosyltransferase and the metal-resistance genes sit on the same chromosomal integrative element. If so, metal resistance should also be elevated beside other carbohydrate-enzyme families near secretion loci, and the signal should disappear in genomes lacking the element.
directions.outcomes: Support: metal-resistance genes lie on the same integrative element as the glycosyltransferase, and the enrichment is specific to this family. Refutation: the enrichment appears equally for other carbohydrate-enzyme families or housekeeping neighbourhoods, or the two gene sets lie on separate elements.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 29572102 and 35230132 describe secretion-system proteins and pan-genomes in single organisms, and 41708296 describes metal-driven resistance spread in wastewater. None tests whether glycosyltransferase neighbourhoods and metal resistance share a mobile element.
directions.question: Why do genomes with glycosyltransferase family 2 genes next to type IV secretion machinery carry far more metal-resistance genes, and does one mobile element carry both?
directions.readiness_basis: Genome annotations are in the lakehouse, but the synteny-threshold test and mobile-element calls on unfiltered data are pending, and closed-genome confirmation needs new long-read sequencing.
directions.test: In Pangenome Collection genomes, take those with glycosyltransferase family 2 within 10 kb of secretion-machinery genes. Compare their metal-resistance content with genomes holding other carbohydrate-enzyme families near secretion loci and with genomes holding housekeeping-gene neighbourhoods as a matched background. Use integrative-element and mobile-element calls on the same contigs, and the 8-phylum tree branch flagged as the strongest transfer event, to test whether metal-resistance genes share the element. Then sequence selected strains with long reads to obtain closed genomes and confirm the arrangement.
directions.title: Do glycosyltransferase genes near secretion loci travel on integrative elements carrying metal resistance?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether secretion-linked integrative elements move cell-surface carbohydrate enzymes between phyla together with metal tolerance. That would tie horizontal transfer of surface chemistry to adaptation in contaminated habitats. Otherwise the association is a by-product of genome quality or habitat.

directions.hypothesis: Openness is a lineage-level tolerance for foreign DNA. Within a phylum, openness should predict prophage markers, resistance genes and mobile-element genes alike, while a non-mobile accessory category such as housekeeping variants should show no such link.
directions.outcomes: Support: openness predicts all mobile categories and their gain rates within phyla but not the non-mobile control. Refutation: openness tracks only one category, or none once relatedness is modelled, which would make the within-phylum positives a lineage artefact.
directions.prior_work: PMID 34983386 links openness to phylogenetic placement across 12 pathogen species and PMID 30576310 links capsules to larger pan-genomes with more prophages and resistance genes. Neither compares several mobile categories against a non-mobile control within lineages.
directions.question: Within a single phylum, do species with more open pangenomes carry more of every kind of mobile gene, including prophages and resistance genes, or only some?
directions.readiness_basis: Species-level openness, resistance and prophage tables exist; gain and loss modelling on the species tree has not been run.
directions.test: Using the Pangenome Collection, within each phylum relate openness to resistance-gene count, prophage marker density and mobile-element gene count. Add a non-mobile accessory category as a negative control, with genome count and phylogenetic relatedness modelled. Estimate gain and loss rates on the species tree for each category to ask whether openness predicts acquisition rate or only present-day content.
directions.title: Are open pangenomes a general permissive state for mobile DNA or only resistance?
directions.why_it_matters: Across all species pooled, openness and resistance are essentially unrelated, yet the link is positive in most tested phyla. A general permissive state would make openness a predictor of how fast a lineage acquires new resistance. Specificity would instead point to selection on resistance.

directions.hypothesis: The deletion benefit is an artefact of shaken rich medium. In sand or soil-like structured culture, or in mixed community culture, the same core genes become important, which would explain why selection keeps them.
directions.outcomes: Support: flagellar and other core-burden genes lose their deletion benefit or become important in structured or competitive culture, more than matched accessory genes. Refutation: the benefit persists unchanged, so the cost is real and conservation has another explanation.
directions.prior_work: PMID 22448042 predicts loss of costly dispensable functions and 22761588 treats selection-driven gene loss, while 29769716 reports mutant phenotypes in laboratory conditions. None tests conserved but laboratory-costly genes in structured or competitive settings.
directions.question: Core genes in motility, RNA metabolism and protein metabolism are more often beneficial to delete than accessory genes are. Do those benefits vanish or reverse in structured, competitive environments?
directions.readiness_basis: Existing browser data are all from laboratory media, so structured and competitive conditions require new library experiments.
directions.test: In the Fitness Browser, list core genes in motility and chemotaxis, RNA metabolism and protein metabolism whose deletion helps in some conditions. Then run barcoded transposon libraries of two or three organisms from the browser in shaken rich medium, in sand- or soil-matrix culture, and in competition with a second species. Compare each gene's fitness across the three settings against accessory genes with similar lab cost.
directions.title: Are conserved genes that help when deleted in rich medium needed in structured habitats?
directions.why_it_matters: It would test directly whether conservation reflects selection in nature that laboratory fitness assays miss. If the benefit persists in structured habitats, these genes may be genuinely costly and kept by other forces.

directions.hypothesis: Defense genes are gained at a rate similar to other function classes but lost quickly. Recent gains of CRISPR-Cas should therefore be less likely than recent gains of other classes to persist into sister clades or deeper nodes.
directions.outcomes: Support: defense gains have shorter persistence than gains of other classes at similar depth, with comparable per-branch gain rate. Refutation: persistence is similar across classes, so the recent skew reflects a true higher acquisition rate or a depth-estimation bias.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 10097118 and 37232518 argue that gene complexity limits transfer, and 21298028 shows transfer drives protein-family expansion. None separates acquisition rate from loss for defense systems.
directions.question: CRISPR-Cas gene families show most of their gains at genus level and very few ancient gains. Is that because they are gained at a high rate, or because gains are lost quickly so only recent ones remain?
directions.readiness_basis: Gain-depth estimates exist per class; persistence of gains was not computed and requires a descendant-presence pass over the tree.
directions.test: Using the acquisition-depth estimates over the species tree, compare CRISPR-Cas, restriction systems and tRNA synthetases. For each gain event, ask whether the gene is still present in descendant genomes at successive depths. Add gain-event counts per branch length to separate rate from persistence, and check the same classes among novel and singleton genes in the 32-species comparison.
directions.title: Is recent gain of defense systems fast turnover rather than fast acquisition?
directions.why_it_matters: A recent-skewed profile is usually read as intense transfer. Separating turnover from acquisition would change how acquisition-depth profiles are read for defense, resistance and other mobile functions.

directions.hypothesis: Module-transfer predictions recover the annotated function of known essential genes far more often than random assignment, despite possible functional divergence from the orthologs. If so, predictions for hypothetical essentials are reliable enough to select genes for depletion tests.
directions.outcomes: Support: hidden functions are recovered well above shuffled assignment and depletion phenotypes match the predicted context. Refutation: recovery is near chance, or predictions fail in depletion, meaning the orthologs' module context does not carry over to essential genes because function has diverged.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29769716 supports function proposals from conserved fitness associations among genes that have mutant data, and PMID 36097170 treats strain-dependent essentiality. Neither benchmarks predictions made indirectly for genes that lack fitness data.
directions.question: Hypothetical essential genes cannot be tested by deletion. Are functions inferred from the fitness modules of their non-essential orthologs in other organisms actually right, given that an essential gene's function may have diverged from those orthologs?
directions.readiness_basis: Predictions, ortholog families and essentiality calls exist for the hidden-function benchmark, but the depletion tests need new experiments.
directions.test: Using the Fitness Browser, hide the annotation of essential genes with well-established functions, rerun module transfer through their non-essential orthologs, and score recovery of the correct family, noting cases where the ortholog's module reflects a diverged role. Include the orphan essentials with no orthologs as a case the method cannot reach. Then deplete several top predictions in a tractable organism and check the growth defect predicted by the module context.
directions.title: Can fitness-module transfer correctly predict functions of essential genes of unknown function?
directions.why_it_matters: Essential genes of unknown function are the hardest part of the dark proteome, since they lack fitness data. A tested prediction method, with its failure rate known, would give a route to assign them functions and target them.

directions.hypothesis: The antibiotic-dependent flip toward importance is set by substrate match between the drug and the gene product. Broad-spectrum pumps flip under many antibiotic classes, narrow pumps only under their own drugs, and enzymatic genes only under their specific drug.
directions.outcomes: Support: knockout fitness shifts mainly in matched drug-gene pairs, and the efflux versus enzymatic contrast shrinks once matching is accounted for. Refutation: efflux genes still flip under unmatched antibiotics, or matched enzymatic genes also fail to flip, so mechanism class rather than substrate match drives the pattern.
directions.prior_work: PMID 26203082 shows resistance genes can give an advantage in vivo but does not split the effect by mechanism or drug match; PMIDs 25861385 and 20208551 cover costs of resistance mutations, not condition-matched knockout effects of native genes.
directions.question: Resistance mechanisms showed no detected difference in baseline knockout fitness, yet efflux genes flip toward importance under antibiotics more than enzymatic inactivation genes do. Is that flip set by how well each antibiotic matches the gene product's substrates, rather than by the mechanism class?
directions.readiness_basis: Knockout fitness for resistance genes under antibiotic and non-antibiotic conditions is already compiled for 25 Fitness Browser organisms; drug-spectrum labels must be added from annotations, and the existing classifier leaves some genes (about 25) in an unknown mechanism class.
directions.test: In the Fitness Browser, take the resistance genes with knockout fitness data across the 25 organisms. Label each gene's likely drug spectrum from its annotation, and subdivide efflux genes into narrow-spectrum drug pumps and general multidrug systems. For every antibiotic experiment, mark whether the drug lies in the gene's expected spectrum. Compare the change in knockout fitness for matched versus unmatched drug-gene pairs, separately for efflux and enzymatic genes. Include organism as a grouping term so the large gene sets in Cupriavidus and BFirm do not dominate.
directions.title: Do efflux genes matter under antibiotics only when the drug matches their substrates?
directions.why_it_matters: Mechanism class did not predict baseline fitness, but efflux and enzymatic genes differ once antibiotics are present, and about 43% of resistance genes do not flip at all. If substrate match explains this, a gene's value could be predicted from the drugs it covers, which would change how resistance maintenance is modelled in mixed-drug environments.

directions.hypothesis: Hotspot cells reflect real geochemical enrichment, so the share of genomes with metal resistance rises with measured metal concentration across independent studies within a cell. Hotspots resting on a single study's samples fall away once sampling effort is controlled.
directions.outcomes: Support: several independent studies in a hotspot cell show raised prevalence, and prevalence rises with the matching measured metal. Refutation: prevalence is driven by one study, or does not rise with measured metal once study is accounted for.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29715297 links arsenic resistance to a natural arsenic gradient in one Atacama river; PMIDs 38004830 and 41845521 describe genomes from single saline-lake and salt-flat sites. None tests whether a global metal-resistance hotspot survives control for study clustering.
directions.question: Few geolocated environmental genomes carry metal resistance, but a few grid cells, such as the Atacama and Andes region, are hotspots. Do the hotspots track measured metal levels, or do they come from a few intensively sampled studies?
directions.readiness_basis: Genome coordinates and sample accessions exist, but joining them to study identifiers and any metal measurements is a new, sizeable join; whether hotspots survive correction for sampling effort has not been tested.
directions.test: Use the share of genomes carrying at least one metal-resistance type (2.8% of 22,356 genomes with coordinates; 21.8% in the Atacama/Andean hotspot cell of 101 genomes; 11 hotspot cells and 3 coldspot cells overall), not metal resistance as a share of a species' resistance genes (45% aquatic, 44% soil, 6% human gut). Using the Pangenome Collection and NMDC BioSamples, group genomes in each hotspot cell by sampling study and count independent studies. Where NMDC Multi-omics or BioSamples hold metal measurements near the same coordinates, relate prevalence to measured metal at matched sites. Compare hotspot with non-hotspot cells of similar genome count, with study as a grouping term.
directions.title: Do metal-resistance hotspots in environmental genomes follow local metal geochemistry or sampling clusters?
directions.why_it_matters: If hotspots follow geochemistry, genome-based maps of metal resistance could serve as proxies for contamination or natural metal load. If they are sampling artefacts, the apparent soil-over-marine contrast in genome prevalence needs to be rebuilt before anyone interprets it ecologically.

directions.hypothesis: Within a species, genomes isolated from metal-rich or contaminated habitats carry metal-specific genes more often than genomes from clean habitats, and more strongly than they carry general-stress genes.
directions.outcomes: Support: metal-specific genes are more often present in genomes from metal-rich habitats, and more so than general-stress genes. Refutation: presence is unrelated to isolation habitat, or equally related for both gene classes.
directions.prior_work: PMID 42262111 reports trade-offs between core and accessory genomes under stress in one species, and PMID 38948139 links fitness genes to core status in another; neither asks whether metal-specific genes follow isolation habitat within species.
directions.question: In two separate analyses, genes needed only under metals were less often core than genes needed under many stresses. The analyses used different gene sets and definitions, so their core fractions are not directly comparable, but both point the same way. Is the patchy presence of metal-specific genes maintained by isolation from metal-rich habitats within species?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene classes and pangenome presence exist, but most Fitness Browser species have few genomes, habitat labels must be harmonised, and the earlier core fractions rest on differing gene sets, so only well-sampled species can be tested.
directions.test: For Fitness Browser organisms with deep pangenomes, classify genes as metal-specific, shared across metals, or generally important from knockout fitness, using one fixed definition of core for all classes. For each gene, record presence across genomes of the same species in the Pangenome Collection. Label each genome's habitat from NMDC BioSamples isolation-source metadata. Test, within species, whether presence of metal-specific genes is associated with contaminated or metal-rich isolation sources, relative to general-stress genes. Restrict to species with enough genomes, since most Fitness Browser species have few (median 9).
directions.title: Are metal-specific genes kept patchily in the accessory genome by local metal exposure?
directions.why_it_matters: Lab fitness shows which genes matter under metals but not why they are absent from many genomes. A habitat link would show that metal-specific resistance is maintained by local selection. No habitat link would point to drift or neutral loss and would weaken an ecological reading of the lower core share.

directions.hypothesis: Classical antibiotic-resistance clusters rise with clinical fraction much more steeply than size-matched clusters of unrelated accessory functions and than metal and stress-response clusters from the same catalog.
directions.outcomes: Support: the antibiotic-resistance slope is clearly steeper than every control class and than metal and stress systems. Refutation: control classes or metal and stress systems rise with clinical fraction about as steeply, so the excess is general accessory inflation or catalog breadth.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 38993487 and 38923192 show more resistance genes in clinical strains of single genera, and PMID 25003965 shows resistomes cluster by ecology; none compares the resistance excess against non-resistance accessory classes or against metal and stress systems across species.
directions.question: Clinical-dominated species carry several-fold more resistance-gene clusters, yet the link between clinical fraction and overall accessory share is borderline. Is the clinical excess confined to the resistance catalog, and within it to classical antibiotic resistance rather than metal and stress systems, or do clinical species also carry excess of unrelated accessory gene classes?
directions.readiness_basis: The species-level resistance table and environment labels exist; separating antibiotic from metal and stress clusters and building size-matched control counts across 823 species needs new queries on the pangenome collection.
directions.test: Use the 823 species with at least 5 genomes in at least 2 environments. Split resistance clusters into classical antibiotic-resistance genes and metal or stress systems, mapping mechanisms to an antibiotic-resistance ontology rather than keyword labels. For each species, count clusters of several non-resistance accessory classes, such as metabolic and transport clusters, matched in size. Regress each count on clinical-genome fraction while holding total genome count constant. Compare the slope for antibiotic resistance with slopes for metal and stress systems and for the control classes, and repeat within phylum.
directions.title: Is the resistance-gene excess in clinical species specific, or part of broad accessory-genome inflation?
directions.why_it_matters: Clinical species are also the most sequenced, so the excess could be a side effect of open, well-sampled genomes. The resistance catalog also contains metal and stress systems, so a catalog-wide excess alone would not show antibiotic selection. A steeper rise for classical antibiotic-resistance genes would be the first piece of evidence that clinical gene content is shaped by drug exposure.

directions.hypothesis: Mutants in the unannotated module genes show growth defects in groundwater-like conditions that are absent or weaker in standard lab medium, more often than annotated module members.
directions.outcomes: Support: unannotated module genes show defects specific to groundwater-like conditions at a higher rate than annotated members. Refutation: defects are equally common in lab medium, or absent in both, so module activity classed as field-relevant does not imply field-specific function.
directions.prior_work: PMID 37065130 maps genome-wide fitness of this organism across many lab conditions, and PMID 39259908 identifies groundwater survival genes in a different subsurface bacterium; neither tests unannotated conserved-module genes in this organism under groundwater-like conditions.
directions.question: In Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough, the 21 ecological fitness modules contain 239 genes, of which 52 are unannotated. Do these unannotated genes affect growth under groundwater-like metal, pH and nitrate stress that standard lab-medium screens do not capture?
directions.readiness_basis: The modules and gene lists exist, but fitness data under groundwater-like chemistry are not in the lakehouse.
directions.test: Grow the existing Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough transposon library, or targeted mutants of the 52 genes, in a medium built from Oak Ridge groundwater chemistry with uranium, low pH and nitrate, and in standard lab medium. Measure barcode-based fitness for the unannotated and annotated module members and for heavy-metal genes. Compare defect rates between conditions and between gene groups.
directions.title: Do unannotated genes in field-relevant conserved modules matter for survival in contaminated groundwater?
directions.why_it_matters: Lab nutrient genes were as core-enriched as field-stress genes, so conservation does not tell field-relevant genes apart. Direct phenotypes for unannotated members would show whether these modules encode real environmental adaptations and would give functions to unannotated genes.

directions.hypothesis: The extra gene content in deep-clay Bacillota_B is mostly transport, regulatory and mobile-element genes. Genomes with the most amino-acid pathway gaps carry the most matching uptake transporters, which points to dependence on neighbours rather than self-sufficiency.
directions.outcomes: Support: transporter and regulatory classes dominate the enriched gene content, pathway gaps track transporter counts, and the isolate needs the supplied amino acids. Refutation: the extra content is mostly biosynthetic or mobile, the pathway gaps do not track transporters, or the pattern comes from one genus alone.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 38902796, 32252814 and 40054447 tie groundwater and deep habitats to smaller genomes; this asks what a larger deep-clay genome contains and whether it signals metabolic dependence.
directions.question: Deep-clay Bacillota_B genomes are larger than soil relatives, yet the quality-filtered deep-clay genomes were less complete for amino-acid synthesis pathways than soil baseline genomes. Where does the extra DNA go, and does it replace synthesis with uptake?
directions.readiness_basis: Anchor and baseline genomes, orthogroup presence and pathway completeness are already in the pangenome collection; only the growth test needs new work, and the small anchor sets limit the analysis.
directions.test: Within Bacillota_B in the Pangenome Collection, sort the many orthogroups enriched in the deep-clay anchor genomes into functional classes. Compare deep-clay and soil genomes on amino-acid pathway gaps and on matching amino-acid transporter counts. Run it per genus (BRH-c8a, BRH-c4a, Desulfosporosinus), because the 10-genome anchor set is dominated by a few genera. The pathway comparison rests on only 6 quality-filtered deep genomes against 137 baseline genomes, and the 18-pathway measure has a ceiling (most cultured organisms score 17-18 of 18), so also score pathway gaps at finer resolution than the 18-pathway count. Then grow a cultured Desulfosporosinus isolate in defined medium with and without single amino acids.
directions.title: Do larger deep-clay Bacillota_B genomes trade biosynthesis for transporters and partner dependence?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that deep-subsurface genome growth can go with metabolic dependence, not only streamlining. That challenges the usual picture of compact, self-sufficient subsurface cells.

directions.hypothesis: Deep-clay Bacillota_B carry flavin-based extracellular electron transfer genes more often than soil Bacillota_B. These genes would account for iron reduction where the cytochrome markers show no deep-versus-shallow difference.
directions.outcomes: Support: flavin-pathway genes are more common in deep-clay genomes and the isolate reduces Fe(III) in a way that tracks them. Refutation: the genes are equally common in soil genomes, or the isolate does not reduce Fe(III).
directions.prior_work: PMID 37642485 reports iron reducers in rock-associated clay communities, and PMIDs 35100867, 30266730 and 34669448 study multi-heme transfer; none asks which route clay Bacillota_B use.
directions.question: After correcting the iron-reduction markers, deep and shallow clay genomes no longer differ, yet rock-associated clay communities are reported to be dominated by iron reducers. Do clay Bacillota_B use an electron-transfer route the cytochrome markers miss?
directions.readiness_basis: Genomes are available, but profile searches for a new gene set must be built and run, and the isolate test needs wet-lab work.
directions.test: Search the anchor and baseline Bacillota_B genomes in the Pangenome Collection and KBase Genomes for flavin-binding extracellular electron transfer gene sets, using sequence profiles rather than the multi-heme markers. Compare deep, shallow and soil groups. Then test a cultured Desulfosporosinus or related clay isolate for Fe(III) reduction with and without a flavin-pathway inhibitor or knockout.
directions.title: Do deep-clay Bacillota_B reduce iron through flavin-based electron transfer rather than multi-heme cytochromes?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that the cytochrome-based marker survey was blind to the real iron-reduction route in a major clay lineage. Iron reduction would then need to be reassessed for repository-relevant clays.

directions.hypothesis: Measured tolerance to individual metals does not follow catalase or urease status within a class. Where a phenotype appears to matter, its effect is explained by the number of metal-resistance gene clusters.
directions.outcomes: Support: once cluster number is in the model, phenotype status adds nothing to measured tolerance within classes. Refutation: catalase-negative or urease-positive strains show reproducibly different measured tolerance for specific metals, such as nickel for urease, beyond what cluster number explains.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 32683159 and 17183702 link catalase to metal resistance in single settings, and PMID 20380737 links urease to nickel transport in one organism; none tests the phenotype across paired strains within a class.
directions.question: Catalase-negative species score higher on predicted metal tolerance inside several classes, though the pooled trend is the opposite, and urease positivity lowers the score only in Actinomycetes. Is that reversal real tolerance, or an artefact of the genome-based score?
directions.readiness_basis: Strain pairs can be chosen from the lakehouse, but no independent per-metal tolerance measurements exist for them.
directions.test: From the Phenotype Collection and Pangenome Collection, pick strain pairs within Gammaproteobacteria and Actinomycetes that differ in catalase or urease status, without matching on metal-resistance cluster number, so that cluster number varies across the set. Measure growth-inhibiting concentrations of copper, nickel, zinc and cadmium for each strain. Model measured tolerance with phenotype status and cluster number together, and compare with predicted scores. Also check against measured metal fitness in the Fitness Browser where an organism overlaps.
directions.title: Do catalase and urease status predict measured metal tolerance within a bacterial class?
directions.why_it_matters: The score is a genome-based prediction, so lineage structure could be producing these phenotype associations. Measured data would show whether phenotype screening of metal tolerance has any use beyond lineage identity.

directions.hypothesis: Most gains of new metal-resistance types happen after a lineage has already broadened its habitat range. Metal diversity is then a consequence of exposure, not a cause of niche expansion.
directions.outcomes: Support: metal-type gains cluster on branches after habitat gains. Refutation: gains of metal types come first, or the two are unrelated once the tree is considered.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 35643011 and 27717408 relate metal contamination and resistance diversity to communities; this asks about the order of events within lineages.
directions.question: Genera resisting more metal types occupy broader niches, but the link weakened under a stricter prevalence filter, and habitat range itself is strongly inherited. Does metal-type diversity arise before habitat expansion or after it?
directions.readiness_basis: Genome-level metal-resistance calls and isolation-source metadata exist, but habitat classes are noisy and the tree-based gain-ordering analysis has to be built.
directions.test: On the genome tree in the Pangenome Collection, reconstruct gains of metal-resistance types and of habitat categories in the same genera, taking habitat categories from genome isolation-source metadata since the occurrence-based habitat counts behind the original finding are not in the listed collections. Test whether gains of habitat categories precede or follow gains of metal types along branches. Use soil enrichment and marine depletion of resistance in geolocated environmental genomes as an independent check of habitat dependence.
directions.title: Does carrying many metal-resistance types let lineages widen their habitat, or follow it?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, metal-resistance repertoires cannot be used to predict which lineages will spread, and co-selection ideas that treat metals as drivers of expansion would need revising.

directions.hypothesis: Taxa abundant in alkaline soils are disproportionately from clades lacking close genomes, and this holds after accounting for how many samples were sequenced per pH range.
directions.outcomes: Support: the unmatched share rises with pH even with sampling effort matched. Refutation: the share is flat across pH once sampling is matched, so the gap is only a sampling effect.
directions.prior_work: PMID 38722174 describes genomic fingerprints of soil ecosystems; this asks whether pH marks lineages with no genomic coverage.
directions.question: Poorly mapped soils are about 0.8 pH units more alkaline than well-mapped ones, and models of soil gene content fail on new data. Do alkaline soils harbour whole lineages absent from genome collections, rather than just fewer sequenced samples?
directions.readiness_basis: Soil pH and taxon profiles are present, but taxon-to-genome matching and sampling-effort matching must be built.
directions.test: Assign taxa from soil samples in NMDC Multi-omics and NMDC BioSamples to the Pangenome Collection, noting taxa with no close genome match. Compare the share of unmatched taxa across pH bins, matching by number of samples per bin and sampling region.
directions.title: Do alkaline soils hold lineages that have no sequenced genome yet?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate a true biological blind spot from a sampling gap, and direct isolation and sequencing effort toward alkaline soils.

directions.hypothesis: Within genera that contain both, hcnC and nifH co-occur less often than expected, and deleting the hcn operon from a diazotroph raises nitrogenase activity and growth without a nitrogen source.
directions.outcomes: Support: co-carriage is rarer within genera than expected, and the hcn deletion raises nitrogenase activity and nitrogen-free growth. Refutation: co-carriage is as common as expected within genera and the deletion changes neither measure, which would point to separate lifestyles instead.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 41190207, 41612514 and 34352636 report nifH and pqqC only as abundance shifts in metagenomes; none tests co-carriage or a mechanism.
directions.question: The nitrogenase gene nifH is negatively associated with the cyanide-synthesis gene hcnC and the PQQ gene pqqC across genomes. Does the cyanide operon impair nitrogen fixation when both sit in one strain, or do the two traits simply belong to different lifestyles?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene presence for nifH, hcnC and pqqC across genomes is already analysed; the within-genus test uses the same data, and the deletion test needs new work.
directions.test: In the Pangenome Collection, take genera containing both nifH and hcnC carriers. Test whether co-carriage is rarer than expected within genus and within soil habitat. Then, in a Pseudomonas or Azotobacter strain, compare acetylene-reduction activity and nitrogen-free growth between the intact strain and an hcn deletion.
directions.title: Does carrying the cyanide operon impair nitrogen fixation in the same strain?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain why plant-growth traits do not stack in one organism and guide the design of inoculants that combine nitrogen fixation with biocontrol.

directions.hypothesis: Fungal replicate variability falls as the amount of inoculum rises. If it persists at high inoculum, priority effects, not sampling of rare propagules, produce it.
directions.outcomes: Support for sampling: spread shrinks with larger inoculum. Support for priority effects: spread persists and the early colonist changes later community makeup. Refutation of both: neither inoculum size nor early colonist changes the spread.
directions.prior_work: PMID 42592007 shows fungal lignin enrichments shaped by temperature and inoculum source; it does not separate sampling chance from priority effects.
directions.question: Bacterial communities responded to lignin enrichment reproducibly while fungal communities varied hugely between replicates. Does fungal chance arise from the few propagules that seed each flask, or from early colonisers shaping what follows?
directions.readiness_basis: The existing enrichment had too few replicates and low fungal read depth, so the question needs new cultures.
directions.test: Repeat the lignin enrichment from the same soil with several inoculum sizes and at least five replicates per size, sequencing fungal markers at matched depth. Compare replicate spread across inoculum sizes. In a second arm, start flasks with an identical early-colonising fungus added first, and compare with flasks without it.
directions.title: Is fungal variability in lignin enrichments chance seeding or priority effects?
directions.why_it_matters: It would tell whether fungal lignin-degrading consortia can be assembled reproducibly by raising inoculum size, or whether they are inherently history-dependent.

directions.hypothesis: Community differences between depths of the same well are explained by layer-specific chemistry (oxygen, nitrate, iron, sulfate), and the weak sideways structure disappears once layer is accounted for. If the plume instead moves laterally, distance along its path will explain community change within a layer.
directions.outcomes: Support: depth and zone explain community change after horizontal distance is removed, and chemistry steps line up with community steps. Refutation: horizontal position along a northeast-to-southwest gradient explains as much as depth within a layer, or geochemistry does not track the community.
directions.prior_work: PMID 30265315 describes hydrologic boundaries shaping subsurface communities and PMID 16407148 shows weak distance effects in soil; neither separates depth from lateral position in a contaminated aquifer with chemistry.
directions.question: Is the strong community change with depth within one well caused by stacked hydrogeological layers with different electron-acceptor chemistry, rather than by a contaminant plume moving sideways?
directions.readiness_basis: Community data exist, but the geochemistry samples are registered and not yet loaded, and the depth-resolved well profile is a new measurement.
directions.test: Using ENIGMA CORAL, compare community dissimilarity against depth difference while holding horizontal distance fixed, and the reverse, within each hydrogeological zone, using a sample list whose counts per zone are fixed first. Then load the registered but not yet loaded geochemistry samples (nitrate, pH, metals, isotopes) and test whether they predict the vertical turnover. Follow with a new depth-resolved geochemical profile in one well to see whether the chemistry steps match the community steps.
directions.title: Do water-table layers, not lateral distance, organize subsurface communities at the Oak Ridge site?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that sampling at the wrong depth, not the wrong well, hides contamination effects at subsurface sites, and it would tell sampling designs where to spend effort. The reported share of sediment variance attributed to zone is uncertain, because the number of samples behind it is stated inconsistently (37 samples versus zone counts of 33, 25, 54 and 45), so the size of the zone effect needs to be re-established within this test.

directions.hypothesis: When groundwater and sediment are sampled together from the same wells, the same taxa remain partitioned, and the partition tracks metabolic lifestyle: iron oxidizers in the water, methane-oxidizing and iron- or sulfur-reducing taxa on solids.
directions.outcomes: Support: the named genera keep their direction of enrichment in simultaneous samples and gene content matches the lifestyle. Refutation: the ratios collapse toward one, showing the earlier contrast came from timing.
directions.prior_work: PMID 22179233 shows Rhodanobacter dominating both groundwater and sediment at this site; the new work tests whether the partition among genera persists when time is controlled and links it to gene content.
directions.question: Do Rhodanobacter, Gallionella and Sideroxydans really prefer flowing groundwater, while Anaeromyxobacter, Arcobacter and Ca. Methanoperedens prefer attached sediment, or does the 18-month gap between sampling create the pattern?
directions.readiness_basis: Existing sediment and groundwater samples were taken 18 months apart, so a simultaneous resampling and shotgun sequencing is required.
directions.test: Collect paired sediment cores and groundwater at the same wells in a single campaign, with 16S profiling and shotgun metagenomes. Compare the abundance ratios of the named genera between materials and check whether genomes of water-enriched versus sediment-enriched taxa carry the inferred iron-oxidation, denitrification, methane-oxidation and sulfate-reduction genes. Use the existing ENIGMA CORAL profiles as the baseline.
directions.title: Is the groundwater-versus-sediment split in Oak Ridge taxa real habitat preference?
directions.why_it_matters: A real partition means groundwater monitoring cannot see the sediment-attached communities that may store and process contaminants. A time artifact would mean the two sample types can be interchanged.

directions.hypothesis: In factorial microcosms, uranium alone at neutral pH does not lower Caulobacter, while low pH or high nitrate does; Herbaspirillum responds to the chemistry rather than to uranium.
directions.outcomes: Support: uranium alone has little effect on Caulobacter in microcosms while pH or nitrate does, and the field uranium signal shrinks with these covariates. Refutation: Caulobacter declines under uranium at neutral pH and low nitrate.
directions.prior_work: PMID 26676055 found Caulobacter growing and dominant with uranium in a synthetic consortium and PMID 30523276 tied Rhodanobacter to uranium by correlation; this adds factorial separation of uranium from pH and nitrate with uranium-free controls.
directions.question: Does uranium directly lower the abundance of Caulobacter and raise Herbaspirillum, or do these field patterns come from co-varying pH, nitrate and carbon?
directions.readiness_basis: Field abundance and uranium data exist, but the uncontrolled covariates require new manipulative microcosms.
directions.test: Build microcosms from Oak Ridge groundwater inocula crossing uranium, pH and nitrate levels, including uranium-free controls, then follow Caulobacter and Herbaspirillum by 16S profiling. Compare with the field abundances in ENIGMA CORAL, fitting uranium with pH and nitrate as joint predictors. Check whether Fitness Browser Caulobacter metal-stress data agree with the direct uranium response.
directions.title: Is uranium itself, or acidity and nitrate, what removes Caulobacter from contaminated wells?
directions.why_it_matters: It would settle whether field correlations with uranium can be read as tolerance or sensitivity, which decides if community composition can be used to monitor uranium. The only lab precedent shows Caulobacter growing in a uranium-containing consortium, not its response relative to an uranium-free control.

directions.hypothesis: Desulfovibrio and other sulfate reducers are enriched in sediment and in isolated anaerobic pockets, so targeted assays show higher abundance there than in groundwater, and the lab results with the model organism describe a minor field member.
directions.outcomes: Support: sulfate reducers are much more abundant in sediment or anaerobic zones than in groundwater. Refutation: they stay rare and undetectable in all material types and depths.
directions.prior_work: PMID 38552495 and PMID 17948804 show sulfate- and uranium-reducing consortia respond to carbon amendment and uranium; they do not ask where in the aquifer the model genus lives unamended.
directions.question: Is Desulfovibrio rare because it is genuinely absent from the aquifer, or because it lives on sediment or in anoxic pockets that groundwater 16S misses, with other sulfate reducers doing its job?
directions.readiness_basis: Community profiles for both materials are in the lakehouse, but the decisive dsrAB assay and deeper sequencing are new measurements.
directions.test: Compare Desulfovibrio and other sulfate-reducer genera between sediment and groundwater profiles in ENIGMA CORAL, noting that the two were sampled at different times. Then run a new sulfate-reducer gene assay (dsrAB) with deeper sequencing on sediment and groundwater from the anaerobic wells, and check whether sulfate-reducer abundance rises in zones where Anaeromyxobacter and Arcobacter dominate.
directions.title: Why is the model sulfate reducer Desulfovibrio nearly absent from Oak Ridge groundwater?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether laboratory work on the favored uranium-reducing model organism transfers to the field, or whether other lineages should be the targets of lab study.

directions.hypothesis: The loss of detectable metabolites in heated mineral soil is concentrated in labile compound classes such as sugars and amino acids, and added labile substrate gives a larger respiration increase in heated than in control soil.
directions.outcomes: Support: losses concentrate in labile classes and heated soil responds more to added substrate. Refutation: losses are spread evenly across classes and substrate addition gives equal responses.
directions.prior_work: Earlier work attributes warming responses to substrate availability and describes community and expression changes in heated forest soil; none examines compound classes in heated mineral soil.
directions.question: Do long-term heated mineral soils have fewer detectable metabolites because the easily used compounds have been consumed, and does adding such substrates restore the microbial response?
directions.readiness_basis: Metabolite lists are in the lakehouse, but the substrate-addition test requires new incubations of heated and control soil.
directions.test: Classify the detected metabolites of heated and control mineral samples by compound class in NMDC Multi-omics and compare class-level losses, since no single metabolite changed on its own. Then add labile substrates to heated and control mineral soil from the same plots and measure respiration.
directions.title: Does warming deplete labile carbon in mineral soil and leave fewer detectable metabolites?
directions.why_it_matters: It would support substrate depletion, not microbial acclimation, as the reason warming effects fade, which affects predictions of long-term soil carbon loss.

directions.hypothesis: Anaerostipes caccae gains no growth or butyrate from lactate made by these pathobionts. Adding them to a defined community will not raise its lactate use or butyrate output, and removing them will not lower butyrate.
directions.outcomes: Support: butyrate and Anaerostipes caccae growth do not depend on the pathobionts, while the positive-control partner does feed it. Refutation: the pathobionts raise its lactate use or butyrate output, or their removal lowers butyrate.
directions.prior_work: PMID 36473601, 33191780 and 18554304 show Anaerostipes caccae using lactate with Bacteroides or Bifidobacterium partners; none tests the Crohn's pathobiont partners that the cohort data implicate.
directions.question: Is lactate from Crohn's-associated gut bacteria such as Flavonifractor plautii and Eubacterium bolteae a real food source for Anaerostipes caccae? If so, removing those bacteria would cost the gut some butyrate.
directions.readiness_basis: It needs anaerobic co-culture and metabolite assays; the cohort correlation is the only existing evidence, it comes from one cohort, and its authors call the status a data-scope limit rather than a refutation.
directions.test: Grow Anaerostipes caccae in defined medium with lactate as the main carbon source, alone and together with Flavonifractor plautii, with Eubacterium bolteae, and with a known lactate-producing partner as a positive control. Measure lactate, butyrate and growth over time. Repeat in a defined multi-species community with and without each pathobiont. Compare with the cohort pattern in which lactate tracked Anaerostipes caccae in the opposite direction from the two pathobionts.
directions.title: Does the butyrate producer Anaerostipes caccae live on lactate made by Crohn's pathobionts?
directions.why_it_matters: A phage cocktail aimed at these pathobionts is judged partly by whether it would starve a beneficial butyrate producer. A cross-feeding link would be a cost of targeting them; its absence would remove that worry.

directions.hypothesis: Strains with siderophore clusters such as yersiniabactin or enterobactin gain a growth advantage over matched non-carrying strains in iron-restricted gut-like medium, and the advantage disappears with added iron. Cluster carriage predicts this better than an adherent-invasive label does.
directions.outcomes: Support: cluster carriers win in iron-restricted medium, the advantage shrinks or disappears with added iron, and it holds regardless of the adherent-invasive label. Refutation: competition outcome tracks the adherent-invasive label or neither trait, or iron level makes no difference.
directions.prior_work: PMID 35359974 measures how common adherent-invasive E. coli is and PMID 28130329 targets it with phage; neither asks whether siderophore and genotoxin cluster carriage gives a competitive edge under varying iron.
directions.question: Do Escherichia coli strains carrying iron-siderophore and genotoxin gene clusters out-compete otherwise similar strains without them when iron is restricted, as in inflamed gut, and does that edge vanish when iron is supplied?
directions.readiness_basis: Genome scoring can run on lakehouse genomes, but the competition assays need new wet-lab work; the existing enrichment is against the full gene-cluster catalog and is inflated by background rarity.
directions.test: From E. coli genomes in KBase Genomes and the Pangenome Collection, score each genome for iron-siderophore and genotoxin cluster carriage and for adherent-invasive markers. Select pairs that differ in one class but not the other. Run pairwise anaerobic competition assays in gut-like medium across an iron series, including an iron-chelated condition, and count each strain by barcode or marker PCR.
directions.title: Do iron-scavenging gene clusters give Escherichia coli a growth edge when iron is scarce?
directions.why_it_matters: Only 8 of 23 Crohn's patients in the UC Davis cohort carried detectable E. coli, so adherent-invasive E. coli may not describe most patients. The iron and genotoxin clusters were strongly enriched among the core gene clusters, but against the full catalog rather than a matched set. A direct growth test would show whether these clusters confer a real ecological advantage, which bears on which strains phage or iron-directed therapy should target.

directions.hypothesis: At least some of the top metabolites on the axis are made in pure culture by the pathobionts that load on it, while others are produced by non-pathobiont members of the community.
directions.outcomes: Support: a substantial share of the axis metabolites appear in pathobiont cultures and fall when the pathobionts are dropped from the community. Refutation: the axis metabolites are absent from pathobiont cultures and unaffected by their removal.
directions.prior_work: PMID 39250478 and 21761941 link microbiota and metabolites by canonical correlation, but only as associations; neither tests whether the named species produce the metabolites.
directions.question: Are the metabolites that load with the six core pathobionts on the joint species-metabolite axis produced by those species, or only correlated with them?
directions.readiness_basis: It needs cultured isolates and a metabolomics run; the axis itself comes from a pilot analysis that its authors say is not a substitute for a full three-modality analysis.
directions.test: Grow the six core pathobionts, singly and in a pooled community, in a stool-derived anaerobic medium. Run untargeted metabolomics on the supernatants and compare them with the metabolites loading on the axis in the paired metagenome and metabolome data. Compare the pooled community with a version lacking the pathobionts.
directions.title: Do the Crohn's-linked pathobionts themselves make the metabolites that separate Crohn's from non-IBD?
directions.why_it_matters: The axis separates Crohn's from non-IBD, but a correlation cannot say whether removing the pathobionts would change the metabolite profile. Production by the pathobionts would make the axis a mechanism-linked readout; absence would mean it tracks community state instead.

directions.hypothesis: The Crohn's association of a candidate species depends on community state: species called in one state are not Crohn's-enriched when the same species are examined in the other state. Placing a candidate in an altered community in a gnotobiotic host changes its expansion.
directions.outcomes: Support: candidates are Crohn's-enriched only in their own state, and the same species expands more in the matching defined community. Refutation: candidates show the same Crohn's direction in both states and expand equally in either synthetic background, meaning the association is species-intrinsic.
directions.prior_work: PMID 28130329 targets a single pathobiont group in Crohn's and PMID 39244168 surveys microbiome differences between populations; neither asks whether one species' disease association depends on its community state.
directions.question: Are Crohn's candidate species disease-linked because of their own properties, or because of the community state (ecotype) they sit in, so that the same species is Crohn's-enriched in one state and neutral in another?
directions.readiness_basis: The state-specific lists exist, but the second state has only one eligible sub-study with provisional candidates, and the gnotobiotic step needs new experiments.
directions.test: Step 1, on existing cohort data: for each species on the first-state and second-state candidate lists, estimate its Crohn's-versus-non-IBD direction within the other state, using only sub-studies with both groups, and ask whether the two lists agree in direction or are state-specific. Note that 45 of 51 first-state candidates kept the same direction in a held-out cohort, and the second-state list is provisional because only one sub-study qualifies. Step 2: colonize germ-free mice with a defined community mimicking each state plus one candidate species such as Flavonifractor plautii or Escherichia coli, and measure expansion of the candidate under an inflammatory challenge in each background.
directions.title: Does the same gut species become Crohn's-associated only inside a particular community state?
directions.why_it_matters: The two states pick very different target lists, and a permutation check against shuffled labels showed that this divergence is not chance. If association is state-dependent, targeting should be decided per community state and not per species. If it is species-intrinsic, the state partition adds nothing to target choice.
